title: AP Computer Science A
description: Free AP Computer Science A study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Java Basics & Primitive Types

concepts.intro: Java source code (.java) is compiled by javac into bytecode (.class), which the JVM executes, making Java platform-independent.
b: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { } } is the required entry point.
Every .java file's public class name must match the filename exactly (Main.java -> class Main).
javac Main.java produces Main.class; java Main runs it via the JVM.
Java is statically typed: every variable's type is declared and checked at compile time.
A missing semicolon or unmatched brace causes a compile-time error, not a runtime error.

concepts.intro: AP CSA uses int for whole numbers and double for decimal (floating-point) numbers as the two primary numeric types.
b: int stores 32-bit whole numbers, e.g. int x = 5;
double stores double-precision decimals, e.g. double pi = 3.14159;
Integer division truncates: 7 / 2 evaluates to 3, not 3.5.
Mixing types promotes to the wider type: 7 / 2.0 evaluates to 3.5.
Casting: (double) 7 / 2 gives 3.5; (int) 3.9 gives 3 (truncates, does not round).
The modulus operator % returns the remainder: 7 % 2 is 1.

concepts.intro: A variable must be declared with a type before use, and assignment stores a value into that variable's memory location.
b: Declaration: int score; Assignment: score = 90; Combined: int score = 90;
Variable names are case-sensitive and conventionally use camelCase (totalScore, not TotalScore).
Compound assignment operators: x += 5 means x = x + 5; also -=, *=, /=, %=.
Increment/decrement: x++ and x-- change a variable by 1.
boolean stores only true or false and is used for logical conditions.
String is not primitive; it's a reference type representing text, e.g. String name = "Ada";

concepts.intro: String objects represent immutable sequences of characters and support several key methods tested on the AP exam.
b: Concatenation with + joins strings: "Hi" + "there" produces "Hithere".
str.length() returns the number of characters, e.g. "hello".length() is 5.
str.substring(a, b) returns characters from index a up to (not including) b.
str.charAt(i) returns the character at index i (0-indexed).
str.equals(other) checks value equality; == checks reference equality (a common trap).
str.indexOf("x") returns the index of the first occurrence, or -1 if not found.

concepts.intro: Java evaluates expressions following a strict order of operations, similar to standard math precedence rules.
b: Parentheses first, then unary (-, ++, --), then *, /, %, then +, -, then relational, then logical.
* / % have equal precedence and evaluate left to right: 8 / 4 * 2 = 4, not 1.
Operator precedence determines order but associativity determines direction for equal-precedence ops.
System.out.println(2 + 3 + "4") prints "54" because 2+3 evaluates first, then concatenates with "4".
System.out.println("4" + 2 + 3) prints "423" because left-to-right string concatenation happens first.

concepts.intro: Java provides wrapper classes like Integer and Double to treat primitives as objects, and ints have a fixed range that can overflow.
b: Integer.MAX_VALUE is 2147483647; adding 1 to it overflows to Integer.MIN_VALUE (a wraparound bug).
Autoboxing automatically converts int to Integer and back when needed, e.g. in ArrayList<Integer>.
Double.parseDouble("3.14") and Integer.parseInt("42") convert Strings to numeric types.
Math.pow(base, exp), Math.sqrt(x), and Math.abs(x) are common static Math class methods.
Math.random() returns a double in [0.0, 1.0); (int)(Math.random() * n) gives a random int in [0, n).

keyFacts: int / int always truncates toward zero; cast one operand to double to get a decimal result.
String comparison must use .equals(), never == (== compares object references, not content).
Java is case-sensitive: int, String, and boolean must be lowercase/exact-case keywords.
Every statement ends in a semicolon; blocks of code are grouped with { }.
traps: Using == to compare Strings, not .equals() — == checks if two references point to the same object.
Expecting 5 / 2 to equal 2.5, not 2 — integer division truncates the decimal part entirely.
Forgetting that (int) casting truncates toward zero, not rounds — (int) 4.9 is 4, not 5.
Confusing = (assignment) with == (equality comparison) inside conditions.

units.name: Objects & Classes

concepts.intro: A class defines the instance variables (state) and methods (behavior) that every object created from it will have.
b: Instance variables are declared inside the class but outside any method, typically private.
private restricts access to within the class only, enforcing encapsulation.
An object is a specific instance of a class, created with the new keyword.
class Dog { private String name; private int age; } defines a Dog blueprint with two fields.
Each object has its own copy of instance variables, independent of other objects of the same class.

concepts.intro: A constructor initializes a new object's instance variables and shares its name with the class.
b: public Dog(String n, int a) { name = n; age = a; } is a constructor for class Dog.
Constructors have no return type, not even void.
The keyword this refers to the current object, e.g. this.name = name; resolves naming conflicts with parameters.
If no constructor is written, Java provides a default no-argument constructor automatically.
You can overload constructors: multiple constructors with different parameter lists in the same class.

concepts.intro: Getters (accessors) return the value of a private field, and setters (mutators) change it, preserving encapsulation.
b: public int getAge() { return age; } is a standard accessor (getter).
public void setAge(int a) { age = a; } is a standard mutator (setter).
Encapsulation means keeping fields private and exposing controlled access via public methods.
Getters/setters let a class validate data (e.g. reject negative age) before changing state.
toString() is a special method that returns a String representation of an object, often overridden.

concepts.intro: A method's signature is its name plus parameter types, and Java allows multiple methods with the same name if signatures differ.
b: public void bark(int times) and public void bark() are overloaded methods (different parameter lists).
Return type alone does NOT distinguish overloaded methods — parameter lists must differ.
Method parameters are passed by value: primitives are copied, and object references are copied (but point to the same object).
A void method returns nothing; a method with a return type must return a matching value on every path.
public static methods belong to the class itself, not an instance, and are called like ClassName.method().

concepts.intro: A variable of an object type stores a reference (memory address) to the object, not the object itself, which leads to aliasing.
b: Dog a = new Dog("Rex", 3); Dog b = a; makes b an alias — both point to the same Dog object.
Changing b.setAge(5) also changes what a.getAge() returns, since they reference the same object.
null means a reference variable points to no object; calling a method on null throws a NullPointerException.
Two references are == only if they point to the exact same object in memory.
Passing an object to a method passes the reference, so the method can mutate the object's fields.

concepts.intro: A class can extend another class to inherit its fields and methods, forming an 'is-a' relationship (fully explored in Unit 7).
b: class Puppy extends Dog { } makes Puppy inherit Dog's public and protected members.
super() calls the parent class's constructor and must be the first line in the subclass constructor.
protected members are accessible in the class, subclasses, and same package.
Overriding a method means redefining a parent method in the subclass with the same signature.
@Override is a common annotation (not required by AP exam) that flags an intentional override.

keyFacts: Constructors share the class name and have no return type, including no void.
this.field = parameter is the standard fix when a constructor parameter shadows a field name.
Objects are compared for identity with ==, but for logical equality you should use .equals().
Private fields are only directly accessible inside their own class's methods.
traps: Writing a constructor with a return type (even void) — this makes it a regular method, not a constructor.
Forgetting this. when a parameter name matches a field name, causing the field to never actually update.
Assuming Dog b = a; copies the object — it only copies the reference; both variables alias the same object.
Comparing objects with == expecting value equality instead of reference equality.

units.name: Boolean Logic & Ifs

concepts.intro: Relational operators compare values and produce a boolean, while logical operators combine boolean expressions.
b: Relational operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= compare numeric values and return true/false.
Logical AND (&&): both sides must be true for the whole expression to be true.
Logical OR (||): true if at least one side is true.
Logical NOT (!): flips a boolean's value, e.g. !true is false.
&& and || use short-circuit evaluation: if the left side of && is false, the right side is never evaluated.

concepts.intro: Conditional statements let a program execute different code blocks depending on whether a boolean expression is true.
b: if (condition) { ... } else { ... } executes one branch or the other, never both.
else if chains test conditions in order; only the first true branch executes.
Conditions must be boolean expressions; Java does not allow if (1) like C does.
Nested if statements place one if inside another to test compound conditions.
Braces {} are optional for single-statement blocks but recommended to avoid dangling-else bugs.

concepts.l: De Morgan's Laws and Compound Conditions
concepts.intro: De Morgan's Laws describe how to negate compound boolean expressions, a frequently tested exam skill.
b: !(A && B) is equivalent to (!A || !B).
!(A || B) is equivalent to (!A && !B).
Negating a relational operator flips it: !(x > 5) is equivalent to x <= 5.
Complex conditions can be simplified using truth tables to verify equivalence.
De Morgan's Laws are commonly tested by asking which expression is logically equivalent to a negated compound condition.

concepts.intro: Comparing primitive values with == checks their actual value, but comparing objects with == checks reference identity, not content.
b: For primitives (int, double, boolean), == correctly compares values.
For objects (String, custom classes), == compares whether two references point to the same object.
String s1 = "cat"; String s2 = "cat"; s1 == s2 may be true due to String pooling, but this is unreliable — always use .equals().
new String("cat") == "cat" is false because new forces a distinct object.
compareTo() returns negative, zero, or positive to indicate ordering, e.g. "apple".compareTo("banana") is negative.

concepts.intro: The ternary operator ?: is a compact way to write a simple if-else that produces a value.
b: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse; e.g. int max = (a > b) ? a : b;
The ternary operator's result can be assigned directly to a variable or printed.
Ternary expressions can be nested, but this quickly becomes hard to read.
Both branches must produce compatible types for the assignment to work.
Ternary operators are common in short evaluations but not required by the AP exam.

concepts.intro: A truth table exhaustively lists every input combination and the resulting output, used to verify or compare boolean expressions.
b: For && there are 4 rows; only T,T yields true.
For || there are 4 rows; only F,F yields false.
Exclusive or (XOR) behavior can be built with (A || B) && !(A && B).
Two expressions are logically equivalent if their truth tables match on every row.
AP free-response questions sometimes ask you to trace boolean expressions with specific variable values.

keyFacts: && and || short-circuit: the right operand may never execute if the left already determines the result.
Always use .equals() for String/object content comparison; == is for primitives and reference identity.
De Morgan's Laws: !(A&&B) == (!A||!B) and !(A||B) == (!A&&!B).
A boolean-valued condition is required inside if(), while(), and the middle clause of for().
traps: Using = instead of == inside a condition, which assigns rather than compares (and often won't compile for non-boolean types).
Comparing Strings with ==, not .equals() — this trap resurfaces constantly across units.
Misapplying De Morgan's Law by forgetting to flip the relational operator along with the connective.
Assuming short-circuit && still evaluates the right side even when the left side is false — it does not.

units.name: Iteration Loops

concepts.intro: A while loop repeats a block of code as long as its boolean condition remains true, checked before each iteration.
b: while (condition) { ... } — the condition is checked before the loop body runs each time.
If the condition is false initially, the loop body never executes (0 iterations possible).
The loop variable must be updated inside the body, or the loop runs forever (infinite loop).
while (true) { ... break; } is a common pattern for loops with an exit condition inside the body.
while loops are ideal when the number of iterations isn't known in advance.

concepts.intro: A for loop packages initialization, condition, and update into one line, ideal for a known number of iterations.
b: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { ... } initializes i, checks i < n before each pass, then increments i after.
The loop runs n times for i = 0, 1, ..., n-1 (classic 0-indexed counting).
for (int i = n; i > 0; i--) counts downward from n to 1.
Any of the three for-loop clauses can be omitted, but the semicolons must remain.
Nested for loops (a loop inside a loop) are used for 2D array traversal and pattern printing.

concepts.intro: A do-while loop executes its body once before checking the condition, guaranteeing at least one execution.
b: do { ... } while (condition); checks the condition AFTER running the body.
Useful when code must run at least once regardless of the condition, e.g. menu prompts.
do-while loops are less common on the AP exam than while and for but still testable.
The semicolon after while (condition) in a do-while is required (a common syntax slip).
Off-by-one behavior differs from while: a do-while with a false condition still runs once.

concepts.intro: break exits a loop entirely, while continue skips to the next iteration without finishing the current one.
b: break immediately terminates the nearest enclosing loop (or switch).
continue skips the rest of the current iteration's body and jumps to the loop's update/condition check.
In a for loop, continue still executes the increment (i++) before re-checking the condition.
Overusing break/continue can make loop logic harder to trace; AP favors clear conditions when possible.
break only exits the innermost loop it's directly inside, not outer loops in nested structures.

concepts.intro: Off-by-one errors occur when a loop iterates one time too many or too few, often due to boundary condition mistakes.
b: for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) runs n+1 times, which often causes an IndexOutOfBoundsException on arrays of size n.
The safe array-traversal bound is i < arr.length, not i <= arr.length.
Changing < to <= (or vice versa) in a loop condition is a classic single-character bug.
Tracing a loop by hand with a small example (n=3) quickly reveals off-by-one mistakes.
Reversed iteration for (int i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) correctly visits every valid index.

concepts.intro: An accumulator pattern uses a loop to build up a running result, such as a sum, count, product, or maximum.
b: int sum = 0; for (int x : arr) { sum += x; } accumulates a running total.
int count = 0; for (...) { if (condition) count++; } counts matching elements.
double product = 1; ... product *= x; is the multiplicative accumulator pattern (starts at 1, not 0).
Finding a maximum: initialize max to the first element (or a very small value), then compare and update.
Accumulator variables must be declared and initialized BEFORE the loop begins, not inside it.

keyFacts: while checks its condition before running; do-while checks after, guaranteeing at least one execution.
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) is the standard safe way to traverse an array by index.
break exits the loop entirely; continue skips only to the next iteration.
A sum accumulator starts at 0; a product accumulator starts at 1.
traps: Using <= instead of < in an array loop bound, causing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Forgetting to update the loop control variable, creating an infinite loop.
Initializing an accumulator inside the loop instead of before it, resetting it every iteration.
Assuming do-while behaves like while — do-while always executes its body at least once.

units.name: Arrays

concepts.intro: An array is a fixed-size, ordered collection of elements of the same type, indexed starting at 0.
b: int[] nums = new int[5]; creates an array of 5 ints, all initialized to 0.
int[] nums = {1, 2, 3}; creates and initializes an array literal in one step.
Array length is fixed at creation; nums.length gives the size (no parentheses — it's a field, not a method).
Valid indices range from 0 to length - 1; accessing arr[arr.length] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Array elements default to 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, and null for object types.

concepts.intro: Arrays are commonly traversed with a standard for loop (for index access) or an enhanced for-each loop (for read-only access).
b: for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) gives index-based access, needed when modifying elements.
for (int x : arr) { ... } is the enhanced for-each loop; x is a copy, so you cannot modify arr through it.
Reversing an array in place swaps arr[i] and arr[arr.length-1-i] for i from 0 to length/2.
Searching linearly checks each element in order until a match is found or the array ends.
The for-each loop cannot access the index, only the value, so use a regular for loop when the index matters.

concepts.intro: Several standard algorithms — linear search, finding min/max, and sum/average — appear frequently on the AP exam.
b: Linear search: loop through checking arr[i] == target; return index if found, -1 if the loop finishes without a match.
Finding the max: initialize max = arr[0], then compare each subsequent element and update if larger.
Sum and average: accumulate a sum with a loop, then divide by arr.length (cast to double to avoid integer division).
Counting occurrences: loop and increment a counter whenever arr[i] matches a condition.
Checking if an array is sorted: compare each adjacent pair arr[i] <= arr[i+1] across the whole array.

concepts.intro: Arrays are objects in Java, so passing an array to a method passes a reference, allowing the method to modify the caller's array.
b: public static void doubleAll(int[] arr) { for (int i=0; i<arr.length; i++) arr[i] *= 2; } permanently changes the caller's array.
Methods can return arrays: public static int[] makeArray(int n) { ... return result; }
Arrays.toString(arr) converts an array to a printable String like [1, 2, 3].
You cannot resize an array; to 'grow' it, you must create a new, larger array and copy elements over.
System.arraycopy() or a manual loop is used to copy elements between arrays.

concepts.intro: AP CSA requires knowing two O(n^2) sorting algorithms by name and behavior: selection sort and insertion sort.
b: Selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum of the unsorted portion and swaps it into place at the front.
Selection sort makes exactly n-1 swaps regardless of initial order.
Insertion sort builds a sorted portion at the front by taking each next element and shifting it into place.
Insertion sort performs well on nearly-sorted data (fewer shifts needed) while selection sort's work is constant.
Both selection sort and insertion sort run in O(n^2) time in the worst case.

concepts.intro: Binary search efficiently finds a target in a SORTED array by repeatedly halving the search range, running in O(log n) time.
b: Binary search requires the array to already be sorted; it fails on unsorted data.
Compare the target to the middle element: if equal, found; if target is smaller, search the left half; if larger, search the right half.
int mid = (low + high) / 2; is the standard midpoint calculation.
Binary search runs in O(log n) time, dramatically faster than linear search's O(n) on large arrays.
The loop/recursion ends when low > high (not found, return -1) or the target is located.

keyFacts: Array indices run from 0 to arr.length - 1; arr.length has no parentheses (it's a field).
Arrays are reference types: passing one to a method lets that method modify the original array's contents.
Binary search requires a sorted array and runs in O(log n); linear search works unsorted in O(n).
Selection sort always makes n-1 swaps; insertion sort's work depends on how sorted the data already is.
traps: Using arr.length() with parentheses — for arrays it's arr.length, a field, not a method call.
Off-by-one with < vs <= in array loop bounds, causing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Running binary search on an unsorted array — it silently gives wrong results instead of erroring.
Assuming a for-each loop (for (int x : arr)) can modify the original array — it only has a copy of each value.

units.name: ArrayLists & References

concepts.intro: ArrayList is a resizable, generic collection class in java.util that grows and shrinks dynamically, unlike fixed-size arrays.
b: ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<String>(); declares and creates an empty ArrayList of Strings.
list.add("cat") appends to the end; list.add(0, "dog") inserts at a specific index.
list.get(i) retrieves the element at index i; list.set(i, val) replaces it.
list.size() returns the number of elements currently stored (like arr.length, but it's a method with parentheses).
ArrayLists only hold objects (reference types), so primitives like int are autoboxed to Integer.

concepts.intro: ArrayLists support insertion and removal anywhere, automatically shifting elements to keep indices contiguous.
b: list.remove(i) removes by index (int argument); list.remove(Object o) removes by value.
list.remove(2) removes the element AT index 2; list.remove(Integer.valueOf(2)) removes the value 2.
Removing or adding elements shifts all subsequent elements' indices, which can break a forward-iterating loop.
list.contains(val) returns true/false; list.indexOf(val) returns the index or -1 if absent.
list.clear() removes all elements, resetting size() to 0.

concepts.intro: Because removal shifts indices, looping forward while removing elements is a classic AP CSA bug; looping backward avoids it.
b: for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) { if (cond) list.remove(i); } can skip elements after a removal.
The fix: iterate backward — for (int i = list.size()-1; i >= 0; i--) — so shifting doesn't skip unvisited elements.
Using a for-each loop while modifying the list throws a ConcurrentModificationException.
An alternative fix is to build a new ArrayList of items to keep instead of removing in place.
size() must be re-checked each loop iteration since it changes as elements are added/removed.

concepts.intro: ArrayLists trade some performance and syntax simplicity for dynamic resizing and built-in convenience methods that arrays lack.
b: Arrays have fixed size set at creation; ArrayLists grow and shrink automatically via add/remove.
Arrays use [] syntax (arr[i]); ArrayLists use method calls (list.get(i), list.set(i, val)).
Arrays can hold primitives directly; ArrayLists require wrapper classes (ArrayList<Integer>, not ArrayList<int>).
Arrays use .length (field); ArrayLists use .size() (method with parentheses).
Converting: many algorithms are easier to write on arrays first, then adapted for ArrayLists.

concepts.intro: Like all objects, ArrayLists are manipulated by reference, so aliasing and pass-by-reference rules from Unit 2 apply here too.
b: ArrayList<String> b = a; makes b an alias of a — modifying b also changes what a sees.
Passing an ArrayList to a method allows that method to permanently modify its contents (add/remove/set).
To make an independent copy, use new ArrayList<>(originalList), which copies references to elements, not a deep copy.
Comparing two ArrayLists with == checks reference identity; use .equals() to check if their contents match.
Wrapper class objects like Integer should be compared with .equals() or unboxed for value comparison, not ==, for values outside the small cached range.

concepts.intro: Many array algorithms — search, sum, filter — translate directly to ArrayLists using get() and size() instead of [] and length.
b: Linear search: for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) if (list.get(i).equals(target)) return i;
Sum: for (int x : list) sum += x; works because ArrayList<Integer> auto-unboxes in arithmetic.
Filtering into a new list: create ArrayList<T> result, loop through source, add matching elements.
Finding max: track a running max object, compare using .compareTo() for Comparable types like Integer or String.
Removing all elements matching a condition safely requires backward iteration or list.removeIf() (not always covered but useful).

keyFacts: ArrayList uses .size() (a method) while arrays use .length (a field) — mixing these up is a compile error.
ArrayList<Integer> can only hold Integer objects, not primitive int, due to Java generics restrictions.
list.remove(int) removes by index; list.remove(Object) removes by matching value — overload ambiguity with Integer is a classic trap.
Removing elements while iterating forward with indices can skip elements; iterate backward to remove safely.
traps: Calling list.length instead of list.size() — ArrayLists never use .length.
Removing elements in a forward for loop, which skips the element that shifts into the just-vacated index.
Writing list.remove(2) when meaning to remove the value 2 from an ArrayList<Integer> — it removes the element AT index 2 instead.
Assuming a for-each loop can be used to remove elements — it throws ConcurrentModificationException.

units.name: 2D Arrays & Inheritance

concepts.intro: A 2D array is an array of arrays, commonly visualized as a grid with rows and columns, indexed as arr[row][col].
b: int[][] grid = new int[3][4]; creates a grid with 3 rows and 4 columns, all initialized to 0.
int[][] grid = {{1,2},{3,4},{5,6}}; creates and initializes a 2D array literal with 3 rows of 2 columns each.
grid.length gives the number of rows; grid[0].length gives the number of columns in row 0.
Nested for loops traverse a 2D array: outer loop for rows, inner loop for columns — for (int r=0;r<grid.length;r++) for (int c=0;c<grid[r].length;c++).
Rows in a 2D array can have different lengths (a 'ragged' or jagged array) since each row is itself a separate array.

concepts.intro: The order in which nested loops iterate rows and columns changes the order elements are visited, though not which elements exist.
b: Row-major traversal: outer loop over rows, inner loop over columns — visits grid[0][0], grid[0][1], ... row by row.
Column-major traversal: outer loop over columns, inner loop over rows — visits grid[0][0], grid[1][0], ... column by column.
Summing an entire 2D array requires visiting every [r][c] pair exactly once, in either traversal order.
Diagonal traversal (grid[i][i]) only works cleanly on square (n x n) grids.
AP free-response often asks to trace or write nested-loop code that processes only part of a grid (e.g. one row).

concepts.intro: A subclass inherits fields and methods from a superclass using extends, modeling an 'is-a' relationship between classes.
b: class Cat extends Animal { } makes Cat a subclass of Animal, inheriting its public/protected members.
super(args) calls the superclass constructor and must be the very first statement in the subclass constructor.
super.methodName() explicitly calls the superclass's version of a method (useful when overriding).
A subclass does NOT inherit private fields/methods directly, but can access them through inherited public/protected methods.
Every class in Java implicitly extends Object if no other superclass is specified.

concepts.intro: Overriding lets a subclass provide its own implementation of a method inherited from its superclass, enabling polymorphic behavior.
b: An overriding method must have the same name, parameter list, and a compatible return type as the parent's method.
Animal a = new Cat(); a.makeSound(); calls Cat's overridden makeSound(), not Animal's — this is dynamic (runtime) binding.
Polymorphism means a superclass reference variable can hold subclass objects, and the actual object's type determines which overridden method runs.
Overloading (same name, different parameters) is resolved at compile time; overriding (same signature) is resolved at runtime.
instanceof checks an object's actual runtime type, e.g. if (a instanceof Cat) allows safe downcasting.

concepts.intro: Abstract classes and interfaces define contracts that other classes must fulfill, supporting polymorphism without full implementation.
b: An abstract class (abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); }) cannot be instantiated directly with new.
A subclass of an abstract class must override all abstract methods or itself be declared abstract.
An interface (interface Comparable) specifies method signatures that implementing classes must define, using implements.
A class can implement multiple interfaces but can only extend one superclass (Java has single inheritance for classes).
Comparable<T> requires a compareTo(T other) method, used by Collections.sort() and similar utilities.

concepts.intro: Every Java class inherits from Object, which provides default equals(), toString(), and hashCode() methods that are often overridden.
b: The default Object.equals() checks reference equality (same as ==) unless a class overrides it.
Overriding equals(Object other) lets a class define logical (content-based) equality, e.g. two Points with the same x,y.
toString() is called implicitly by System.out.println(obj) and string concatenation with an object.
A well-written equals() typically checks the parameter's type/cast before comparing fields.
Overriding equals() without overriding hashCode() can cause inconsistent behavior in hash-based collections (a conceptual note, not tested in depth on AP CSA).

keyFacts: 2D array access is grid[row][col]; grid.length is the row count, grid[0].length is the column count of row 0.
super(...) must be the first line of a subclass constructor if used at all.
Overriding requires an identical method signature; overloading requires a different parameter list.
A superclass reference can point to a subclass object, and overridden methods run based on the object's actual type (dynamic binding).
traps: Swapping row and column indices (grid[col][row] instead of grid[row][col]), scrambling the grid's meaning.
Forgetting super(args) must be the first statement, causing a compile error if other code precedes it.
Confusing overriding with overloading — overriding needs the exact same parameters; overloading needs different ones.
Assuming grid[r].length is the same for every row — jagged 2D arrays can have different-length rows.

units.name: Recursion & Algorithms

concepts.intro: A recursive method calls itself to solve smaller instances of the same problem, requiring a base case to stop the recursion.
b: Every recursive method needs a base case (a condition that returns without recursing) to avoid infinite recursion.
The recursive case calls the method again on a smaller/simpler version of the problem, moving toward the base case.
public static int factorial(int n) { if (n == 0) return 1; return n * factorial(n-1); } is a classic example.
Each recursive call gets its own stack frame with its own copies of local variables and parameters.
Missing or unreachable base cases cause a StackOverflowError at runtime.

concepts.intro: Tracing recursion means following each call down to the base case, then following the returns back up, often drawn as a call stack or tree.
b: factorial(4) calls factorial(3), which calls factorial(2), ..., down to factorial(0), which returns 1 directly.
Return values propagate back up: factorial(1)=1*1=1, factorial(2)=2*1=2, factorial(3)=3*2=6, factorial(4)=4*6=24.
Drawing an explicit call stack (each call waiting for the one below it to return) helps avoid trace errors.
Recursive Fibonacci fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) makes TWO recursive calls per non-base case, forming a call tree.
AP free-response frequently asks students to trace a recursive method's output for a specific input by hand.

concepts.intro: Recursion can process Strings and arrays by operating on one element and recursing on the rest (a smaller substring or sub-array).
b: Recursive string reversal: reverse(s) = reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0), with base case s.length() <= 1.
Recursive array sum: sum(arr, i) = arr[i] + sum(arr, i+1), with base case i == arr.length returning 0.
Recursive linear search on an array checks index i, then recurses on i+1 if no match, base case i == arr.length.
Palindrome check recursively compares the first and last characters, then recurses on the substring between them.
Recursion on a String typically shrinks via substring(); recursion on an array typically shrinks via an index parameter.

concepts.intro: Any recursive algorithm can be rewritten iteratively with a loop, and choosing between them is a matter of clarity versus overhead.
b: Recursive solutions are often more concise for problems with a naturally recursive structure (trees, divide-and-conquer).
Iterative solutions avoid the memory overhead of building up many stack frames.
Deep recursion (very large n) risks StackOverflowError, while an equivalent loop does not.
Recursion is required conceptually for algorithms like merge sort, even though loops handle simpler tasks like summing an array.
AP CSA expects you to convert between simple recursive and iterative versions of the same algorithm.

concepts.intro: Binary search can be implemented recursively, recursing into the left or right half of a sorted array based on a midpoint comparison.
b: binarySearch(arr, target, low, high): base case is low > high, returning -1 (not found).
If arr[mid] == target, return mid; if target < arr[mid], recurse on (low, mid-1); else recurse on (mid+1, high).
Each recursive call halves the search space, giving binary search its O(log n) time complexity.
Recursive binary search requires the array to be sorted, same as the iterative version.
int mid = low + (high - low) / 2; avoids potential overflow compared to (low + high) / 2 (a subtle but real detail).

concepts.intro: Merge sort is a recursive, divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm running in O(n log n) time, and Big-O describes algorithm efficiency as input grows.
b: Merge sort recursively splits the array in half, sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves back together.
Merge sort runs in O(n log n) time, faster than selection/insertion sort's O(n^2) for large inputs.
Big-O notation describes worst-case growth rate: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n^2) quadratic.
Linear search is O(n); binary search is O(log n); selection/insertion sort are O(n^2); merge sort is O(n log n).
The merge step combines two already-sorted halves by repeatedly comparing their front elements and taking the smaller.

keyFacts: Every correct recursive method needs a base case and a recursive case that moves toward it.
Recursive calls build a call stack; unreachable base cases cause a StackOverflowError.
Binary search and merge sort both run in O(log n) and O(n log n) respectively, beating linear-time and O(n^2) alternatives.
Big-O order from fastest to slowest growth: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2).
traps: Forgetting the base case entirely, or writing one that's never actually reached, causing infinite recursion.
Tracing recursive calls in the wrong order — remember calls return in reverse (last call in, first to return).
Assuming recursion is always faster than iteration — it often has more overhead due to stack frames.
Mixing up which recursive call handles the 'left half' vs 'right half' in recursive binary search, breaking the search.

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly declares and initializes an int variable named count?
quiz.e: Java uses the lowercase primitive type 'int' and a single '=' for assignment, ending with a semicolon.

quiz.q: What is the result of the expression 7 / 2 in Java, where both operands are int?
quiz.e: Integer division truncates the fractional part, so 7 / 2 evaluates to 3.

quiz.q: What is the result of 7.0 / 2 in Java?
quiz.e: Because one operand (7.0) is a double, Java performs floating-point division, giving 3.5.

quiz.q: What value does the expression 7 % 2 produce?
quiz.e: The modulus operator returns the remainder after division, and 7 divided by 2 leaves a remainder of 1.

quiz.q: Which primitive type is used to store a single character in Java?
quiz.e: 'char' is the primitive type for a single character, enclosed in single quotes, e.g. 'A'.

quiz.q: What is the output of System.out.println(5 + 3 + "apples")?
o: Error: cannot mix int and String
quiz.e: Addition is evaluated left to right, so 5 + 3 becomes 8 first, and then 8 is concatenated with the string to give "8apples".

quiz.q: What is the output of System.out.println("apples" + 5 + 3)?
quiz.e: Once a String is concatenated, the '+' operator performs string concatenation left to right, appending 5 then 3 as text: "apples53".

quiz.q: Which of these is a valid boolean literal in Java?
quiz.e: The boolean literal must be the lowercase keyword true (or false) without quotes.

quiz.q: What data type should be used to store a value like 3.14159 with fractional precision?
quiz.e: double is the primitive type used for floating-point (decimal) numbers in Java.

quiz.q: What is the value of x after: int x = 10; x += 5; x *= 2;
quiz.e: x becomes 15 after x += 5, then 15 * 2 = 30 after x *= 2.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly casts a double value d to an int, truncating any decimal part?
quiz.e: Java requires an explicit cast (int) to convert a double to an int, since it may lose precision.

quiz.q: What is printed by: int a = 5; System.out.println(a++ + " " + a);
quiz.e: Post-increment a++ returns the original value 5 for the print, but then increments a to 6, so the output is "5 6".

quiz.q: What is printed by: int a = 5; System.out.println(++a + " " + a);
quiz.e: Pre-increment ++a increments a to 6 before it is used, so both printed values are 6.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the correct way to declare a constant PI equal to 3.14 that cannot be reassigned?
quiz.e: The 'final' keyword in Java marks a variable as a constant whose value cannot change after initialization.

quiz.q: What happens when you divide an int by 0 in Java, e.g. int x = 5 / 0;?
o: It throws an ArithmeticException at runtime
quiz.e: Integer division by zero throws an ArithmeticException at runtime because there is no valid integer result.

quiz.q: What is the result of 5.0 / 0 in Java?
quiz.e: Floating-point division by zero produces the special value Infinity rather than throwing an exception.

quiz.q: Which expression correctly checks if two int variables a and b are equal?
quiz.e: The '==' operator compares primitive values like ints for equality; '=' is assignment.

quiz.q: What is the order of operations in: int result = 2 + 3 * 4;
quiz.e: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so 3 * 4 = 12 is computed first, then 2 + 12 = 14.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of implicit widening conversion?
quiz.e: Assigning an int to a double is a widening conversion that Java performs automatically without a cast.

quiz.q: What is the data type of the result of (int)(3.9)?
quiz.e: Casting a double to int truncates (does not round) the decimal, so (int)(3.9) evaluates to the int 3.

quiz.q: Which of these variable names is NOT a legal Java identifier?
quiz.e: Java identifiers cannot begin with a digit, so 2total is illegal.

quiz.q: What is the output of: System.out.println(10 == 10.0);
quiz.e: Java automatically widens the int 10 to a double for comparison, and 10.0 == 10.0 is true.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the difference between int and double in Java?
o: int stores whole numbers; double stores numbers with a fractional part
double is used only for boolean logic
int can store decimals but double cannot
quiz.e: int is a whole-number (integer) primitive type, while double stores floating-point numbers with decimal precision.

quiz.q: What is the value of b after: boolean b = (5 > 3) && (2 > 4);
quiz.e: The && operator requires both sides to be true; since 2 > 4 is false, the whole expression is false.

quiz.q: What is the value of b after: boolean b = (5 > 3) || (2 > 4);
quiz.e: The || operator is true if at least one side is true; since 5 > 3 is true, the result is true.

quiz.q: Which code segment correctly uses the Scanner class to read an integer typed by the user?
o: Scanner s = new Scanner(System.in); int x = s.nextInt();
Scanner s = new Scanner(); int x = s.readInt();
Scanner s = System.in; int x = s.nextInt();
quiz.e: A Scanner object is created with 'new Scanner(System.in)' and its nextInt() method reads an integer from input.

quiz.q: What is the output of: System.out.println("5" + 2 + 3);
quiz.e: Once concatenation starts with a String, subsequent '+' operations append text left to right, producing "523".

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly represents integer overflow behavior for int in Java?
o: It wraps around to a very negative number
It rounds to the nearest valid int
quiz.e: Java ints use 32-bit two's complement representation and silently wrap around (overflow) rather than throwing an exception.

quiz.q: What is the value of x after: int x = 3; x = x * x + 1;
quiz.e: x * x evaluates to 3 * 3 = 9, then adding 1 gives x = 10.

quiz.q: Which comment style is used for a multi-line comment in Java?
quiz.e: Java uses /* ... */ to delimit multi-line (block) comments; // is for single-line comments.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to print a value without moving to a new line afterward?
quiz.e: System.out.print() outputs text without appending a newline, unlike println().

quiz.q: What is the output of the following: int x = 5; System.out.println(x > 3 ? "big" : "small");
quiz.e: The ternary operator evaluates the condition x > 3 (true), so it returns the first result, "big".

quiz.q: Which of the following best explains why 0.1 + 0.2 may not exactly equal 0.3 when using double in Java?
o: Java has a bug in addition
Doubles use binary floating-point representation, which cannot exactly represent all decimal fractions
Doubles round all results to whole numbers
The + operator does not work on doubles
quiz.e: Floating-point numbers are stored in binary, and many decimal fractions like 0.1 cannot be represented exactly, causing small rounding errors.

quiz.q: What is the value of num after: int num = 15; num = num % 4;
quiz.e: 15 divided by 4 is 3 remainder 3, so the modulus operator returns 3.

quiz.q: Which keyword is used to declare a method or variable that belongs to the class rather than to any instance?
quiz.e: The 'static' keyword designates a class-level member shared by all instances rather than belonging to one object.

quiz.q: What is printed by: double d = 7 / 2; System.out.println(d);
quiz.e: Since 7 and 2 are both int, integer division occurs first (giving 3), and then 3 is widened to 3.0 when stored in d.

quiz.q: What is the correct fix so that double d = 7 / 2; produces 3.5 instead of 3.0?
quiz.e: Making at least one operand a double, such as 7.0, forces floating-point division before the result is truncated as an int.

quiz.q: Which of the following is equivalent to x = x + 1;?
quiz.e: As standalone statements, x++ and ++x both simply increment x by 1, producing the same effect as x = x + 1;.

quiz.q: What is the result of evaluating !(5 > 3)?
quiz.e: 5 > 3 is true, and the logical NOT operator ! negates it to false.

quiz.q: What is the value of x after: int x = 4; x -= 2; x /= 1;
quiz.e: x -= 2 makes x equal to 2, and dividing by 1 leaves it unchanged at 2.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a constructor in a Java class?
o: To initialize a newly created object's instance variables
quiz.e: A constructor runs when an object is created with 'new' and is used to initialize the object's instance variables.

quiz.q: Given: public class Dog { private String name; public Dog(String name) { this.name = name; } } What does 'this.name' refer to?
o: The instance variable name, distinguishing it from the parameter
quiz.e: 'this.name' explicitly refers to the object's instance variable, which is otherwise shadowed by the parameter also named 'name'.

quiz.q: What access modifier should instance variables typically have to support encapsulation?
quiz.e: Making instance variables private hides internal state from outside classes, which is the core idea of encapsulation.

quiz.q: Which method is automatically called when an object is created using the 'new' keyword?
o: The constructor matching the arguments given
quiz.e: 'new ClassName(args)' allocates memory and invokes the constructor whose parameter list matches the arguments.

quiz.q: What does a 'getter' method typically do in a class that follows encapsulation?
o: Returns the value of a private instance variable
quiz.e: A getter (accessor) method returns the current value of a private field so outside code can read it safely.

quiz.q: What is method overloading?
o: Defining two methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class
Calling a method too many times
Overriding a method in a subclass
quiz.e: Overloading means multiple methods share a name but differ in the number or types of parameters, letting Java pick the right one at compile time.

quiz.q: Given class Point { private int x, y; public Point(int x, int y) {...} public double distance(Point other) {...} } which line correctly creates a Point object at (3, 4)?
quiz.e: Objects are instantiated with the 'new' keyword followed by a call to a matching constructor: new Point(3, 4).

quiz.q: What is returned by a method declared with return type void?
o: Nothing; it performs an action but returns no value
quiz.e: 'void' indicates the method performs some action but does not return any value to the caller.

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly overrides the toString() method to customize how an object prints?
quiz.e: toString() must be declared public, return a String, and take no parameters to properly override Object's toString().

quiz.q: In the class Rectangle with private int width, height; what is the effect of a 'setWidth' mutator method?
o: It changes (mutates) the value of the width instance variable
quiz.e: A mutator (setter) method changes the value of a private instance variable, typically after validating the new value.

quiz.q: What does the keyword 'this' refer to inside an instance method?
o: The current object on which the method was called
quiz.e: 'this' is a reference to the current object instance, useful for distinguishing fields from parameters or passing itself along.

quiz.q: Which of the following is true about instance variables versus local variables?
o: Instance variables are declared inside a method and exist only during that call
Instance variables belong to the object and exist as long as the object does; local variables exist only within their method/block
Local variables can be accessed from any method without being passed
quiz.e: Instance variables persist for the lifetime of the object, while local variables are created and destroyed within the method or block where they're declared.

quiz.q: What is the default value of a private int instance variable if not explicitly initialized?
quiz.e: Instance variables of type int are automatically initialized to 0 by Java if no value is assigned.

quiz.q: What will happen if a class has no explicitly written constructor?
o: Java provides a default no-argument constructor
Java uses the constructor from the superclass only
quiz.e: If no constructor is written, Java automatically supplies a default no-argument constructor that does nothing extra.

quiz.q: Which of these best demonstrates encapsulation in a BankAccount class?
o: private double balance; public double getBalance() { return balance; }
quiz.e: Making balance private and exposing a public getBalance() method controls how the field is accessed, which is encapsulation.

quiz.q: Consider: public class Circle { private double radius; public Circle(double radius) { this.radius = radius; } public double getArea() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; } } What is printed by: Circle c = new Circle(2); System.out.println(c.getArea());
quiz.e: getArea() computes Math.PI * 2 * 2, which is approximately 12.566370614359172.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a class and an object?
o: A class is a blueprint/template; an object is an instance created from that blueprint
An object defines methods; a class stores data
A class can only have one object
quiz.e: A class defines the structure and behavior (blueprint), while an object is a specific instance created from that class using 'new'.

quiz.q: Which method signature correctly represents a no-argument constructor for a class named Car?
quiz.e: A constructor shares the class's name, has no return type (not even void), and here takes no parameters.

quiz.q: What is method overriding?
o: Defining multiple methods with the same name in one class
A subclass providing a new implementation for a method inherited from its superclass
Using the same method name in unrelated classes
quiz.e: Overriding occurs when a subclass redefines a method with the exact same signature as one in its superclass.

quiz.q: Given int[] nums is passed to a method as a parameter, what is passed: the array itself or a copy?
o: A full copy of every element
A reference to the same array in memory
A copy of only the first element
quiz.e: Java passes object references (like arrays) by value, but that value is a reference to the same underlying array object, so changes inside the method affect the original array.

quiz.q: What does 'public' access mean for a method or class?
o: Only the class itself can call it
Only classes in the same package can access it
quiz.e: 'public' access means the member is visible and callable from any other class, regardless of package.

quiz.q: In a class with multiple constructors that differ in parameter lists, what is this called?
quiz.e: Having multiple constructors with different parameter lists in the same class is constructor overloading.

quiz.q: What value does a method with return type boolean need to include?
o: A return statement returning a boolean expression, on every code path
A return statement returning any type
A print statement instead of return
quiz.e: Every code path of a method declared to return boolean must eventually return a value of type boolean.

quiz.q: Given: public class Student { private String name; private int grade; public Student(String name, int grade) { this.name = name; this.grade = grade; } } What must the constructor call look like to create a Student named 'Amy' with grade 90?
quiz.e: The constructor parameters are (String name, int grade) in that order, so the arguments must match: ("Amy", 90).

quiz.q: What is the benefit of writing accessor (getter) and mutator (setter) methods instead of making fields public?
o: It makes the code run faster
It allows validation and controlled access to an object's internal state
It is required by the Java compiler
It removes the need for constructors
quiz.e: Getters and setters let a class validate or restrict how its data is read or changed, protecting the object's internal state.

quiz.q: What keyword indicates a method cannot be overridden by a subclass?
quiz.e: Marking a method 'final' prevents any subclass from overriding it.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a valid instance method header inside a class named Book?
quiz.e: A correct method header lists the access modifier, return type, method name, and parameter list, e.g. public String getTitle().

quiz.q: What does calling obj.equals(other) typically check for objects, if equals() has not been overridden?
o: Whether the two objects have the same field values
Whether the two references point to the exact same object in memory
Whether the objects are of the same class only
quiz.e: The default Object.equals() checks reference equality (same memory location) unless the class overrides equals() to compare field values.

quiz.q: Which statement about static methods is true?
o: They can access instance variables directly without an object
They belong to the class rather than any instance and cannot directly access instance variables
quiz.e: Static methods belong to the class itself, so they cannot directly reference instance variables without an object reference.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following, given a Circle class with getArea() but no toString() override? System.out.println(new Circle(1));
o: A meaningful description of the circle
The class name followed by an @ symbol and a hash code, e.g. Circle@1b6d3586
quiz.e: Without a toString() override, Java uses Object's default, which prints the class name and a hexadecimal hash code.

quiz.q: Which is the correct way to call an instance method getArea() on an object c of type Circle?
quiz.e: Instance methods are called using dot notation on an object reference: c.getArea().

quiz.q: What happens if a subclass constructor does not explicitly call super(...)?
o: Java automatically inserts a call to the superclass's no-argument constructor first
The object is created without calling any superclass constructor
It calls the subclass's own constructor twice
quiz.e: If super(...) is not written explicitly, Java automatically inserts a call to the no-argument superclass constructor as the first statement.

quiz.q: Which of these correctly declares a private instance variable named age of type int?
quiz.e: The correct order is [access modifier] [type] [name];, giving private int age;.

quiz.q: What is the term for hiding a class's internal data and requiring all interaction through methods?
quiz.e: Encapsulation is the object-oriented principle of hiding internal state and exposing controlled access through methods.

quiz.q: Consider: public class Counter { private int count = 0; public void increment() { count++; } public int getCount() { return count; } } What is printed after: Counter c = new Counter(); c.increment(); c.increment(); System.out.println(c.getCount());
quiz.e: Each call to increment() adds 1 to count, so after two calls, count is 2, which getCount() returns.

quiz.q: What is a class's constructor NOT allowed to have?
o: A return type, not even void
The same name as the class
quiz.e: Constructors never declare a return type, not even void; the class name and parameter list are what define them.

quiz.q: If a method parameter has the same name as an instance variable, how do you refer to the instance variable inside that method?
o: Just use the variable name directly
quiz.e: The 'this' keyword disambiguates and accesses the instance variable when a parameter shadows it with the same name.

quiz.q: Which statement about objects being compared with == is TRUE?
o: == compares the values inside the objects
== compares whether two references point to the same object in memory
== always returns true for objects of the same class
quiz.e: For reference types like objects, == checks whether both variables refer to the identical object in memory, not whether their contents are equal.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a class's private helper method?
o: To be called only from outside the class
To break a complex task into a smaller piece used internally by the class's own methods
To store data instead of a variable
quiz.e: A private helper method supports the class's other methods internally and is not intended to be called from outside the class.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to define a method within class Circle that returns the circumference using a private radius field?
o: public double getCircumference() { return 2 * Math.PI * radius; }
public void getCircumference() { return 2 * Math.PI * radius; }
quiz.e: The method must declare a return type (double), a name, and correctly return an expression computing the circumference using the instance field.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int x = 5; if (x > 3) { System.out.println("A"); } else { System.out.println("B"); }
quiz.e: Since x (5) is greater than 3, the condition is true, so the if-branch executes and prints "A".

quiz.q: Which boolean expression correctly checks that x is between 1 and 10, inclusive?
quiz.e: Both bounds must be checked with the AND operator and inclusive comparisons: x >= 1 && x <= 10.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following code? int x = 7; if (x % 2 == 0) System.out.println("even"); else System.out.println("odd");
quiz.e: 7 % 2 evaluates to 1, which is not 0, so the else branch runs and prints "odd".

quiz.q: In a chain of if / else if / else statements, how many branches can execute?
o: All branches whose condition is true
Exactly one branch: the first one whose condition is true, or the else if none match
quiz.e: Java evaluates conditions top to bottom and executes only the first branch found true, skipping the rest; else runs if none matched.

quiz.q: What does the expression !(a && b) evaluate to when a is true and b is false?
quiz.e: a && b is false (since b is false), and negating false with ! gives true (De Morgan's law: !(a && b) equals !a || !b).

quiz.q: According to De Morgan's Laws, !(x > 5 && y < 10) is equivalent to which expression?
quiz.e: De Morgan's law states !(A && B) is equivalent to !A || !B, and negating > 5 gives <= 5, negating < 10 gives >= 10.

quiz.q: What is printed by the following? int score = 85; if (score >= 90) System.out.println("A"); else if (score >= 80) System.out.println("B"); else System.out.println("C");
quiz.e: score (85) fails the first check (>= 90) but passes the second (>= 80), so "B" is printed.

quiz.q: What is a common logic error when using if statements with multiple independent conditions instead of else if?
o: Multiple blocks may execute when only one was intended, since each if is checked independently
It always throws a runtime error
quiz.e: Separate if statements are each evaluated on their own, so more than one block can run, unlike a single if/else if chain where only one branch executes.

quiz.q: What is the value of result after: int a = 4; String result = (a % 2 == 0) ? "even" : "odd";
quiz.e: The ternary operator evaluates a % 2 == 0 (true, since 4 is even) and returns the first value, "even".

quiz.q: Which condition correctly checks whether a String s is NOT equal to "cat" using proper String comparison?
quiz.e: Strings should be compared with .equals() for content equality; !s.equals("cat") correctly checks for inequality of content.

quiz.q: What is the output of: boolean flag = false; if (flag = true) { System.out.println("yes"); } else { System.out.println("no"); }
quiz.e: This is a common bug: using = (assignment) instead of == sets flag to true and the assignment expression itself evaluates to true, so "yes" prints.

quiz.q: Given nested conditionals, what determines which inner if-else executes?
o: The inner if-else only executes if its enclosing (outer) condition is true
Inner conditions are always checked first
Nested conditionals are illegal in Java
quiz.e: Control only reaches a nested if-else block if the surrounding (outer) condition that contains it evaluates to true.

quiz.q: What is the result of the boolean expression: 5 != 5
quiz.e: The != operator checks for inequality; since 5 equals 5, the expression is false.

quiz.q: What is printed by: int x = 10; if (x < 5); { System.out.println("here"); }
o: "here" is printed unconditionally, because of the stray semicolon after the if condition
quiz.e: The semicolon after the if condition creates an empty statement as the if-body, so the following block always executes regardless of the condition—a classic bug.

quiz.q: Which logical operator evaluates its right operand only if needed (short-circuit)?
quiz.e: && and || are short-circuit operators: && skips the right side if the left is false, and || skips it if the left is true.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int x = 0; if (x != 0 && 10 / x > 1) System.out.println("safe"); else System.out.println("skip");
quiz.e: Because && short-circuits, since x != 0 is false, Java never evaluates 10 / x, avoiding division by zero, and prints "skip".

quiz.q: Which expression correctly represents 'x is even AND positive'?
quiz.e: Checking evenness requires x % 2 == 0, and combining with positivity requires the AND operator: x % 2 == 0 && x > 0.

quiz.q: What does the comparison operator >= check?
quiz.e: >= checks whether the left operand is greater than or equal to the right operand.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following? int a = 3, b = 5; if (a > b) { System.out.println("a"); } else if (a < b) { System.out.println("b"); } else { System.out.println("equal"); }
quiz.e: a (3) is not greater than b (5), but a is less than b, so the second condition is true and "b" prints.

quiz.q: What is a truth table used for in boolean logic?
o: Listing all possible input combinations and their resulting boolean output
quiz.e: A truth table enumerates every combination of boolean inputs and shows the resulting output of a logical expression, useful for verifying equivalences.

quiz.q: What is the value of (true || false) && false?
quiz.e: true || false is true, but true && false is false, so the overall expression is false.

quiz.q: What is printed by: int num = -5; if (num >= 0) System.out.println("non-negative"); else System.out.println("negative");
quiz.e: Since num (-5) is not greater than or equal to 0, the else branch runs and prints "negative".

quiz.q: Which is equivalent to the boolean expression !(x == y)?
quiz.e: Negating an equality check == produces the inequality check !=.

quiz.q: What does dangling if-else ambiguity refer to, and how does Java resolve it?
o: Java disallows nested if statements entirely
When an else could match multiple if statements; Java binds it to the nearest unmatched if
quiz.e: In nested if statements without braces, Java's rule is that an else always pairs with the closest preceding if that lacks an else.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int grade = 72; if (grade >= 90) System.out.print("A"); if (grade >= 60) System.out.print("Pass");
quiz.e: These are two independent if statements (not else if), so only the second condition (grade >= 60) is true, printing just "Pass".

quiz.q: Which expression is TRUE only when exactly one of a and b is true (exclusive or)?
quiz.e: The ^ (XOR) operator on booleans returns true only when exactly one of its operands is true.

quiz.q: What is the value of the expression: (3 < 5) == (10 > 2)?
quiz.e: Both (3 < 5) and (10 > 2) evaluate to true, and true == true is true.

quiz.q: Given int x = 4, y = 9; what is the value of (x < y) && (x != 4)?
quiz.e: x < y is true, but x != 4 is false since x equals 4, so the AND of true and false is false.

quiz.q: Why should floating-point numbers generally not be compared for exact equality using ==?
o: == does not work on doubles at all
Floating-point rounding errors can make mathematically equal values differ slightly in representation
It always causes a compile error
quiz.e: Because of how doubles are stored in binary, small rounding errors can make two 'equal' calculations differ slightly, so ranges or tolerances are used instead of ==.

quiz.q: What is printed by: char grade = 'B'; if (grade == 'A') System.out.println("Excellent"); else if (grade == 'B') System.out.println("Good"); else System.out.println("Other");
quiz.e: grade equals 'B', which matches the second condition, so "Good" is printed.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to test if an int variable n is a multiple of both 3 and 5?
quiz.e: A number is a multiple of both 3 and 5 only if the remainder is 0 for both, joined with AND.

quiz.q: What happens if you compare two String objects with == instead of .equals()?
o: It always works correctly for content comparison
It compares whether both variables reference the same object in memory, which can give unexpected false results
quiz.e: == on String objects checks reference identity, not content, so two strings with equal content created differently may compare as not equal with ==.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int n = 15; if (n % 3 == 0 && n % 5 == 0) System.out.println("FizzBuzz"); else if (n % 3 == 0) System.out.println("Fizz"); else System.out.println("Buzz or number");
quiz.e: 15 is divisible by both 3 and 5, so the first condition is true and "FizzBuzz" is printed.

quiz.q: Which statement about else-if chains is correct regarding readability compared to nested if statements?
o: They function identically but else-if often reads more clearly for mutually exclusive conditions
else-if chains cannot use boolean expressions
They cannot include a final else
quiz.e: else-if chains and equivalent nested if-else structures behave the same, but else-if is usually clearer for a sequence of mutually exclusive conditions.

quiz.q: What is the boolean value of (5 > 3) & (2 > 4) using the non-short-circuit & operator?
quiz.e: & still evaluates both operands (no short-circuiting) but produces the same logical AND result: true & false is false.

quiz.q: What does the condition (x > 0) != (y > 0) test for, when x and y are ints?
o: Whether x and y have the same sign (both positive or both non-positive)
Whether x and y have different signs (one positive, one non-positive)
quiz.e: != is true when the two boolean sub-expressions differ, meaning exactly one of x, y is positive—i.e., they have different signs.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int x = 5; if (x = 10) { } — assuming this were legal for int? (Note: in Java this specific case)
o: It compiles and sets x to 10
It causes a compile-time error because an int cannot be used where a boolean is required
quiz.e: Unlike C, Java requires if conditions to be boolean expressions; assigning an int inside the condition produces a compile-time type error.

quiz.q: Which condition correctly checks that a variable age is NOT within the range 13 to 19 (not a teenager)?
quiz.e: To be outside the range, age must be below 13 OR above 19, combined with the OR operator.

quiz.q: What is printed by: boolean a = true, b = false, c = true; System.out.println(a && b || c);
quiz.e: && has higher precedence than ||, so a && b (false) is computed first, then false || c (true) gives true.

quiz.q: In an if-else if-else structure with 3 branches, what is the maximum number of boolean condition evaluations if the first condition is true?
quiz.e: Once the first condition evaluates to true, its branch executes and the remaining conditions in the chain are never evaluated.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following loop? for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { System.out.print(i + " "); }
quiz.e: The loop starts at i=0 and runs while i < 5, printing 0 through 4 before i becomes 5 and the loop stops.

quiz.q: How many times does the following loop execute? for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++)
quiz.e: The loop runs for i = 1, 2, ..., 10, which is 10 iterations, stopping once i exceeds 10.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a while loop and a do-while loop?
o: A do-while loop always executes its body at least once, checking the condition after the first pass
A while loop always executes at least once
They are functionally identical in all cases
quiz.e: A do-while loop checks its condition after executing the loop body, guaranteeing at least one execution, unlike a while loop which checks first.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int sum = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { sum += i; } System.out.println(sum);
quiz.e: The loop adds 1+2+3+4 to sum, resulting in 10.

quiz.q: What causes an infinite loop in: int i = 0; while (i < 5) { System.out.println(i); }
o: The condition i < 5 is always false
i is never modified inside the loop, so the condition remains true forever
while loops cannot use less-than comparisons
quiz.e: Because i is never incremented inside the loop body, i < 5 stays true forever, creating an infinite loop.

quiz.q: What is the output of: for (int i = 5; i > 0; i--) { System.out.print(i + " "); }
quiz.e: Starting at i=5 and decrementing while i > 0 prints 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, stopping before i reaches 0.

quiz.q: What is the value of count after this loop: int count = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { if (i % 2 == 0) count++; }
quiz.e: The even values of i in 0-9 are 0,2,4,6,8, five values, so count is incremented 5 times.

quiz.q: What keyword immediately exits the nearest enclosing loop entirely?
quiz.e: 'break' immediately terminates the nearest enclosing loop or switch statement.

quiz.q: What keyword skips the rest of the current loop iteration and proceeds to the next iteration's condition check?
quiz.e: 'continue' jumps directly to the next iteration, skipping any remaining code in the current pass of the loop.

quiz.q: What is the output of: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { if (i == 2) continue; System.out.print(i); }
quiz.e: When i equals 2, continue skips the print statement for that iteration only, so the output is 0, 1, 3, 4.

quiz.q: What is the output of: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { if (i == 2) break; System.out.print(i); }
quiz.e: When i reaches 2, break exits the loop entirely before printing, so only 0 and 1 have been printed.

quiz.q: What does a nested loop such as: for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < 2; j++) { System.out.print("*"); } } print?
quiz.e: The outer loop runs 3 times, and for each outer iteration the inner loop runs 2 times, printing 3 * 2 = 6 stars total.

quiz.q: What is an off-by-one error in loop design?
o: A syntax error that prevents compilation
A logic error where a loop runs one time too many or too few iterations, often due to boundary conditions like < vs <=
An error only in while loops
An error caused by using continue
quiz.e: Off-by-one errors happen when loop bounds are set incorrectly (e.g., using < instead of <= or starting at the wrong index), causing one extra or missing iteration.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int x = 1; do { System.out.print(x + " "); x++; } while (x <= 3);
quiz.e: The do-while loop executes the body first (printing 1), then checks the condition, continuing to print 2 and 3 before x becomes 4 and the loop stops.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int x = 5; do { System.out.print(x + " "); x++; } while (x < 3);
quiz.e: A do-while loop always executes its body at least once, printing 5 before checking that x < 3 is false and stopping.

quiz.q: What is the value of total after: int total = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { total += i * i; }
quiz.e: The loop sums the squares of 1 through 5: 1+4+9+16+25 = 55.

quiz.q: Which loop structure is generally preferred when the exact number of iterations is known in advance?
quiz.e: A for loop conveniently combines initialization, condition, and update in one line, making it ideal when the number of iterations is known beforehand.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int n = 0; while (n < 3) { for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { System.out.print("x"); } n++; }
quiz.e: The outer while loop runs 3 times, and each time the inner for loop prints 2 x's, for a total of 3 * 2 = 6 x's.

quiz.q: In the enhanced for-each loop 'for (int num : arr)', what does 'num' represent on each iteration?
o: The index of the current element
A copy of the value of the current element in arr
A reference to the entire array
quiz.e: The for-each loop assigns 'num' the value of each element of arr in turn, from first to last, without exposing the index.

quiz.q: Why can't you use a for-each loop to modify the original elements of an int array?
o: for-each loops cannot iterate over arrays
The loop variable holds a copy of each primitive value, so reassigning it does not change the array
It is a syntax error to try
for-each only works with objects, not primitives
quiz.e: Since the loop variable in a for-each loop is a copy of the primitive value, changing that variable does not affect the actual array element.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int product = 1; for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { product *= i; } System.out.println(product);
quiz.e: product accumulates the factorial pattern: 1*1*2*3*4 = 24.

quiz.q: What condition would cause the loop 'for (int i = 10; i >= 1; i -= 2)' to run, and how many times does it iterate?
quiz.e: Starting at 10 and decreasing by 2 while i >= 1 gives the sequence 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 — 5 iterations.

quiz.q: What is a sentinel value in a loop context?
o: A special value used to signal the end of input or looping, checked as the loop's stopping condition
quiz.e: A sentinel value is a predetermined value (like -1 or an empty string) used to signal that a loop reading input should stop.

quiz.q: What happens if the update statement of a for loop, like i++, is accidentally omitted, e.g. for (int i = 0; i < 5;) { System.out.print(i); }?
o: The loop runs infinitely because i never changes
quiz.e: Without an update to i, the condition i < 5 never becomes false, so the loop runs forever (assuming i isn't changed inside the body).

quiz.q: What best describes the purpose of a loop invariant when reasoning about loop correctness?
o: A value that changes every iteration
A condition that remains true before and after each iteration, helping verify the loop behaves correctly
quiz.e: A loop invariant is a property that holds true at the start and end of every iteration, useful for proving a loop achieves its intended purpose.

quiz.q: What is the output of: for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) { for (int j = 1; j <= i; j++) { System.out.print("*"); } System.out.println(); }
o: A triangle: 1 star, then 2 stars, then 3 stars on separate lines
A triangle of 6 stars total on one line
quiz.e: The inner loop's bound depends on i, so it prints 1 star on the first line, 2 on the second, and 3 on the third, forming a triangle pattern.

quiz.q: What is the value of x after: int x = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++) { x++; } }
quiz.e: Both loops run 3 times each, so the inner statement executes 3 * 3 = 9 times, making x equal to 9.

quiz.q: Which loop below is guaranteed to run at least one time regardless of the condition?
quiz.e: A do-while loop executes its body once before ever checking the condition, so it always runs at least once.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int i = 0; while (i < 3) { i++; if (i == 2) continue; System.out.print(i); }
quiz.e: i is incremented first each pass; when i becomes 2, continue skips the print, so the printed values are 1 and 3.

quiz.q: When accumulating a sum in a loop, why must the accumulator variable be initialized before the loop begins?
o: Java automatically initializes all variables to 0
Using an uninitialized local variable causes a compile-time error, and the accumulator needs a known starting value
It is only a style preference, not a requirement
quiz.e: Java requires local variables to be definitely assigned before use, and an accumulator needs a defined starting point (usually 0) to correctly sum values.

quiz.q: What is the result of the following loop meant to find the maximum in an array, if arr = {3, 7, 2, 9, 4}? int max = arr[0]; for (int i = 1; i < arr.length; i++) { if (arr[i] > max) max = arr[i]; }
quiz.e: The loop compares each subsequent element to the running maximum, ultimately finding that 9 is the largest value in the array.

quiz.q: What does 'for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++)' guard against, compared to hardcoding a specific number like 10?
o: It ensures the loop correctly adapts to arrays of any size, avoiding out-of-bounds errors if the array length changes
It only works for arrays of exactly size 10
quiz.e: Using arr.length instead of a fixed number keeps the loop correct even if the array's size changes, preventing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

quiz.q: In nested loops, if a break statement is executed inside the inner loop, what happens?
o: Both the inner and outer loops terminate immediately
Only the inner loop terminates; the outer loop continues to its next iteration
Nothing happens; break only works in switch statements
quiz.e: A plain break only exits the loop it is directly inside; the outer loop resumes normally on its own next iteration.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int count = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) { if (i % 4 == 0) count++; } System.out.println(count);
quiz.e: Multiples of 4 from 1 to 20 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 — five values, so count equals 5.

quiz.q: What is a common purpose of using a boolean flag variable in a while loop?
o: To control when the loop should stop based on some event detected inside the loop, rather than a simple counter
To replace the need for any condition
To make the loop run infinitely
quiz.e: A flag variable can be set to true/false based on some condition discovered during loop execution, and then checked to decide whether to continue looping.

quiz.q: What is the output of: for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { System.out.print(i); if (i < 3) System.out.print(","); }
quiz.e: The comma prints only when i < 3, so it appears after 0,1,2 but not after the final value 3, yielding "0,1,2,3".

quiz.q: Which statement about the scope of a for loop's control variable (e.g., i in for (int i...)) is correct?
o: i is accessible after the loop finishes
i is only accessible within the for loop's own block and cannot be used after the loop ends
i must be declared outside the loop
quiz.e: A variable declared in the for loop's initialization is scoped only to that loop; it cannot be referenced once the loop has ended.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int sum = 0; int i = 1; while (i <= 100) { sum += i; i++; } (conceptually, what does sum equal?)
quiz.e: This loop sums all integers from 1 to 100, which by the well-known formula n(n+1)/2 equals 100*101/2 = 5050.

quiz.q: Which of the following best explains why 'while (true) { ... break; ... }' is sometimes used intentionally?
o: It creates a loop that runs until an internal condition triggers a break, useful when the exit condition is easier to check mid-loop than at the top
quiz.e: This pattern is used when the natural place to check for the stopping condition is in the middle of the loop body rather than at the very start.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int i = 0; while (i < 3) { System.out.print("*"); i++; }
quiz.e: The loop runs while i < 3, executing for i=0,1,2 (three times), printing three asterisks.

quiz.q: How do you correctly declare and create an int array of size 5 in Java?
quiz.e: Java arrays are declared with type[] name and created with 'new type[size]', e.g. int[] arr = new int[5];

quiz.q: What is the index of the last element in an array declared as int[] arr = new int[10];?
quiz.e: Array indices start at 0, so an array of length 10 has valid indices 0 through 9.

quiz.q: What exception is thrown when accessing arr[10] on an array of length 10?
quiz.e: Index 10 is out of bounds for an array with valid indices 0-9, causing an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

quiz.q: What is the default value of each element in a newly created int[] array of size 3?
