quiz.e: Java automatically initializes numeric array elements (like int) to 0.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int[] arr = {1, 2, 3}; System.out.println(arr.length);
quiz.e: The 'length' field of an array gives its total number of elements, which is 3 for this array.

quiz.q: Which loop correctly prints every element of int[] arr using indices?
o: for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++) System.out.println(arr[i]);
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) System.out.println(arr[i]);
for (int i = 1; i < arr.length; i++) System.out.println(arr[i]);
for (int i = 0; i < arr.length(); i++) System.out.println(arr[i]);
quiz.e: The loop must start at index 0 and use < arr.length (not <=) to correctly cover all valid indices without going out of bounds.

quiz.q: Given int[] arr = {5, 10, 15}; what is the value of arr[1]?
quiz.e: Array indices start at 0, so arr[0] is 5, arr[1] is 10, and arr[2] is 15.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following code meant to sum an array's elements? int[] arr = {2, 4, 6}; int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) { sum += arr[i]; } System.out.println(sum);
quiz.e: The loop adds each element: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12.

quiz.q: What does the enhanced for-each loop 'for (int x : arr)' do?
o: Iterates over each element of arr in order, assigning it to x, without needing an index
Only works with the first element
Requires arr to be sorted first
quiz.e: The for-each loop automatically iterates through every element of the array in order and assigns each to the loop variable.

quiz.q: What is the result of trying to change an array element using a for-each loop, e.g. for (int x : arr) { x = 0; }?
o: It sets every element of arr to 0
It has no effect on the original array, since x is a copy of each element's value
It only changes the first element
quiz.e: In a for-each loop, the loop variable is a copy of the primitive value, so modifying it does not change the actual array.

quiz.q: How do you find the maximum value in an int[] arr assuming it's non-empty?
o: Initialize max = arr[0], then loop through comparing and updating max when a larger element is found
quiz.e: The standard algorithm starts with the first element as a candidate maximum, then scans the rest, updating max whenever a bigger value is found.

quiz.q: What is a linear search algorithm used for with arrays?
o: Sorting an array in ascending order
Checking each element sequentially from the start until the target is found or the array ends
quiz.e: Linear search checks each element one at a time in order, comparing to the target value, and works regardless of whether the array is sorted.

quiz.q: What is a requirement for using binary search on an array?
o: The array must contain only positive numbers
The array must have an even length
The array must be reversed first
quiz.e: Binary search relies on repeatedly halving the search range based on comparisons, which only works correctly if the array is already sorted.

quiz.q: In binary search on a sorted array, what happens after comparing the target to the middle element and finding the target is larger?
quiz.e: If the target is greater than the middle element, it must be in the right half (since the array is sorted), so the search continues there.

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of linear search in the worst case for an array of n elements?
quiz.e: In the worst case, linear search may need to examine every one of the n elements, giving O(n) time complexity.

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
quiz.e: Binary search halves the search space each step, leading to a logarithmic O(log n) time complexity.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int[] arr = new int[4]; arr[0] = 1; arr[1] = 2; System.out.println(arr[2] + arr[3]);
quiz.e: Elements arr[2] and arr[3] were never assigned, so they retain their default value of 0, and 0 + 0 = 0.

quiz.q: Which algorithm repeatedly finds the smallest remaining element and places it at the front, one position at a time?
quiz.e: Selection sort repeatedly selects the minimum element from the unsorted portion and swaps it into its correct sorted position.

quiz.q: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly compares and swaps adjacent elements until the array is sorted?
quiz.e: Bubble sort works by repeatedly stepping through the array, swapping adjacent elements that are out of order.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of selection sort and bubble sort on an array of size n?
quiz.e: Both selection sort and bubble sort use nested loops that together perform roughly n^2 comparisons in the worst case.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following code that reverses an array in place? int[] arr = {1,2,3,4}; for (int i = 0; i < arr.length/2; i++) { int temp = arr[i]; arr[i] = arr[arr.length-1-i]; arr[arr.length-1-i] = temp; } What is arr now?
quiz.e: The loop swaps elements from the outside in (index i with index length-1-i), fully reversing the array to {4,3,2,1}.

quiz.q: Given int[] a = {1,2,3}; int[] b = a; b[0] = 99; what is a[0] after this code?
quiz.e: Arrays are reference types, so 'b = a' makes b refer to the same array object as a; modifying through b also changes what a sees, so a[0] becomes 99.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to make an independent copy of an array arr so that changes to the copy don't affect the original?
quiz.e: Arrays.copyOf(arr, arr.length) creates a genuinely new array with the same elements, unlike simple assignment which just copies the reference.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int[] arr = {4, 2, 7, 1}; Arrays.sort(arr); System.out.println(arr[0] + " " + arr[3]);
quiz.e: Arrays.sort() sorts the array in ascending order to {1,2,4,7}, so arr[0] is 1 (smallest) and arr[3] is 7 (largest).

quiz.q: What is a common off-by-one bug when initializing an array using its length as a bound, such as new int[arr.length + 1] versus new int[arr.length]?
o: Choosing the wrong size can leave an extra unused 0-valued slot or cause an index out-of-bounds error elsewhere
There is no possible bug here
It always causes a compile error
quiz.e: Miscounting the required size by one (e.g., forgetting +1 or adding an unnecessary +1) is a classic source of bugs involving unused slots or missing space.

quiz.q: What does the following code compute for int[] arr = {3, 1, 4, 1, 5}; int count = 0; for (int x : arr) { if (x == 1) count++; }
quiz.e: The value 1 appears twice in the array, so count is incremented twice, ending at 2.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int[] arr = {10, 20, 30}; for (int i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) { System.out.print(arr[i] + " "); }
quiz.e: Starting from the last index and decrementing prints elements in reverse order: 30, 20, 10.

quiz.q: What causes a NullPointerException when working with an array of objects, e.g. String[] names = new String[3]; System.out.println(names[0].length());?
o: Each element defaults to null for object arrays, and calling a method on a null reference throws this exception
Strings cannot be stored in arrays
quiz.e: Object array elements (like String) default to null, not empty values, so calling .length() on an unassigned element throws a NullPointerException.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the parameter in a method like public static int sum(int[] arr)?
o: To return a copy of arr
To accept a reference to an existing array so the method can process its elements
To create a brand-new array named arr
To declare arr as a local variable only
quiz.e: The method parameter receives a reference to the caller's array, allowing the method to read (and potentially modify) its elements.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int[] arr = {1,2,3,4,5}; int target = 3; boolean found = false; for (int x : arr) { if (x == target) found = true; } System.out.println(found);
quiz.e: The loop checks every element and sets found to true when it encounters 3, which is present in the array.

quiz.q: Which statement about multi-declaration array literals like int[] arr = {1, 2, 3}; is true?
o: This syntax is only valid at the point of declaration, not for later assignment
This creates an array of length 4
This is a syntax error in Java
quiz.e: Array initializer syntax like {1, 2, 3} can only be used when declaring the array; you cannot use it later with arr = {1,2,3};, you would need new int[]{1,2,3}.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to assign a new array to an already-declared variable arr after initial declaration?
quiz.e: After the initial declaration, reassigning requires the explicit 'new int[]{...}' form rather than the bare initializer list.

quiz.q: What does it mean for an algorithm to be in-place, like many array-based sorts?
o: It requires creating an entirely new array for output
It rearranges elements within the original array using only a small constant amount of extra memory
It only works on sorted input
quiz.e: In-place algorithms modify the original data structure directly, without needing significant additional storage proportional to input size.

quiz.q: What happens when linear search is used to find a value that does not exist in an array?
o: It examines every element without finding a match, and typically returns a sentinel like -1
quiz.e: Linear search checks every element; when the target isn't present, the search completes the whole array and conventionally signals failure with a value like -1.

quiz.q: Given a sorted array {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14}, what is the first middle index binary search checks (using low=0, high=6)?
quiz.e: Binary search computes mid = (low + high) / 2 = (0 + 6) / 2 = 3 as the first index examined.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following code that computes the average of an array? int[] arr = {2, 4, 6}; int sum = 0; for (int x : arr) sum += x; double avg = sum / arr.length; System.out.println(avg);
quiz.e: sum (12) divided by arr.length (3, an int) gives integer division result 4, but assigning to a double widens it to display as 4.0.

quiz.q: Which of these correctly counts how many elements in an int[] arr are negative?
o: int count = 0; for (int x : arr) { if (x < 0) count++; }
int count = 0; for (int x : arr) { if (x > 0) count++; }
int count = arr.length; for (int x : arr) count--;
quiz.e: This code correctly increments count only when an element x is less than 0 (negative).

quiz.q: What is a key limitation of using a fixed-size array to store a growing collection of data?
o: Once created, an array's size cannot change; a larger array must be created and elements copied over to add more room
Arrays cannot be passed to methods
quiz.e: Arrays have a fixed length once created; increasing capacity requires allocating a new, larger array and copying the existing elements into it.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int[] a = {1,2,3}; int[] b = {1,2,3}; System.out.println(a == b);
quiz.e: a and b are two distinct array objects with the same contents, but == on arrays compares references, not contents, so it returns false.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following code that computes the sum of only positive numbers in an array? int[] arr = {-2, 5, -1, 8, 3}; int sum = 0; for (int x : arr) { if (x > 0) sum += x; } System.out.println(sum);
quiz.e: The positive numbers in the array are 5, 8, and 3, and 5 + 8 + 3 = 16.

quiz.q: What is stored in an ArrayList<Integer> versus an int[] array in terms of flexibility?
o: Both have fixed size after creation
An ArrayList can grow and shrink dynamically, while a plain array has a fixed size
Arrays can grow dynamically but ArrayLists cannot
quiz.e: Unlike arrays, ArrayList automatically resizes itself as elements are added or removed, offering more flexibility.

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly declares an empty ArrayList of Strings?
quiz.e: The correct generic syntax declares and instantiates with matching type parameters: ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<String>();

quiz.q: Which method adds an element to the end of an ArrayList<String> named list?
quiz.e: The add() method appends an element to the end of an ArrayList.

quiz.q: Which method retrieves the element at index 2 of an ArrayList<Integer> named list?
quiz.e: ArrayList uses the get(index) method to retrieve an element, since it doesn't support array-style bracket indexing.

quiz.q: Which method returns the number of elements currently in an ArrayList?
quiz.e: ArrayList uses the size() method (not the .length field used by arrays) to report its current number of elements.

quiz.q: What happens to the indices of elements after list.remove(2) is called on an ArrayList?
o: All elements after index 2 shift down by one index to fill the gap
A gap remains at index 2 permanently
quiz.e: Removing an element from an ArrayList shifts all subsequent elements one position earlier to keep the list contiguous.

quiz.q: What is autoboxing in the context of ArrayList<Integer>?
o: Manually converting int to Integer using a cast
The automatic conversion Java performs between a primitive type (like int) and its wrapper class (like Integer)
quiz.e: Autoboxing is Java's automatic conversion of primitive values to their corresponding wrapper objects (e.g., int to Integer) when needed, such as when adding to an ArrayList<Integer>.

quiz.q: Why can't you create an ArrayList<int> in Java?
o: Generic type parameters must be reference (wrapper) types, not primitives; use ArrayList<Integer> instead
quiz.e: Java generics require object types, so primitives like int cannot be used directly as type parameters; the wrapper class Integer is used instead.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following? ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<Integer>(); list.add(10); list.add(20); list.add(1, 15); System.out.println(list);
quiz.e: add(1, 15) inserts 15 at index 1, shifting 20 to index 2, resulting in [10, 15, 20].

quiz.q: How do you correctly iterate through all elements of an ArrayList<String> list using a for-each loop?
quiz.e: The enhanced for-each loop syntax 'for (Type var : collection)' works with ArrayLists just as with arrays, here using String s : list.

quiz.q: What is the result of calling list.set(0, 99) on an ArrayList<Integer> where list = [5, 10, 15]?
quiz.e: set(index, value) replaces the existing element at that index with the new value, so index 0 (which held 5) becomes 99, giving [99, 10, 15].

quiz.q: What does list.contains("apple") return for an ArrayList<String>?
o: true if the list contains an element equal to "apple", false otherwise
quiz.e: contains() returns a boolean indicating whether the list has at least one element equal (via equals()) to the specified value.

quiz.q: What is a common bug when removing elements from an ArrayList while iterating forward with a for loop, such as removing based on a condition?
o: Elements shift down after removal, so the next index may skip an element that should also be checked
It always throws a compile error
quiz.e: Because remaining elements shift to fill the gap after a removal, continuing to increment the index can cause the loop to skip over the next element.

quiz.q: What is the safest general approach to avoid skipping elements when removing items from an ArrayList during iteration?
o: Iterate backward from the end of the list toward the beginning
Never remove elements from an ArrayList
quiz.e: Iterating backward means that removing an element only affects indices already processed, avoiding the skip issue that occurs when iterating forward.

quiz.q: Which best explains the concept of an object reference in Java, as opposed to a primitive value?
o: A reference stores the actual object data directly, like a primitive
A reference stores the memory location (address) that points to where the actual object data is stored
References are the same as primitives
quiz.e: Unlike primitives which hold their value directly, reference variables hold an address pointing to the object's data stored elsewhere in memory.

quiz.q: What is the result of: ArrayList<Integer> a = new ArrayList<Integer>(); a.add(1); ArrayList<Integer> b = a; b.add(2); System.out.println(a);
quiz.e: Since b = a copies the reference, both a and b point to the same ArrayList object, so adding to b also affects what a sees: [1, 2].

quiz.q: What does list.isEmpty() return for an ArrayList that has zero elements?
quiz.e: isEmpty() returns true exactly when the list's size is 0.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following code that removes all even numbers from an ArrayList by iterating backward? ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(1,2,3,4,5,6)); for (int i = list.size()-1; i >= 0; i--) { if (list.get(i) % 2 == 0) list.remove(i); } System.out.println(list);
quiz.e: Iterating backward and removing each even element safely leaves only the odd numbers: [1, 3, 5].

quiz.q: What is the difference between remove(int index) and remove(Object o) for ArrayList<Integer>?
o: remove(int) removes the element at that index; remove(Object) removes the first element equal to that object's value
remove(int) removes by value, not index
quiz.e: Due to overloading, remove(int) treats its argument as an index, while remove(Object) (e.g., remove(Integer.valueOf(5))) searches for and removes a matching value.

quiz.q: What is printed by: ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<String>(); list.add("a"); list.add("b"); list.add("c"); list.remove("b"); System.out.println(list);
quiz.e: remove("b") removes the first element equal to the String "b", leaving [a, c].

quiz.q: Which of the following describes how ArrayList achieves its dynamic resizing internally?
o: It is backed by an array that Java automatically replaces with a larger array (copying elements) when capacity is exceeded
It cannot resize, hence the fixed-size limitation
quiz.e: Internally, ArrayList maintains a backing array; when it becomes full, a new larger array is created and existing elements are copied over automatically.

quiz.q: What is aliasing in the context of Java references?
o: Two different variables referring to the same underlying object, so changes through one affect the other
quiz.e: Aliasing occurs when multiple reference variables point to the same object in memory, meaning modifications via any alias are visible through all of them.

quiz.q: What does 'ArrayList<Integer> copy = new ArrayList<Integer>(original);' do?
o: Makes copy an alias of original
Creates a new ArrayList containing copies of the references/values from original, independent of the original list structure
quiz.e: Passing a collection to the ArrayList constructor creates a new list with the same elements, so structural changes (add/remove) to one don't affect the other.

quiz.q: What is the output of: ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<Integer>(); for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) list.add(i * i); System.out.println(list.get(2));
quiz.e: The list holds squares [1, 4, 9, 16, 25], so index 2 (the third element) is 9.

quiz.q: What exception is thrown by list.get(10) if the ArrayList only has 5 elements?
quiz.e: ArrayList's get() method throws an IndexOutOfBoundsException (a broader exception than the array-specific one) for invalid indices.

quiz.q: Which statement about wrapper classes like Integer, Double, and Boolean is true?
o: They are primitives just like int, double, boolean
They are object representations of primitive types, needed for use in generic collections like ArrayList
They cannot store any numeric value
They replace the need for primitives entirely
quiz.e: Wrapper classes wrap a primitive value in an object, which is required because Java generics only work with reference types.

quiz.q: What is the output of comparing two Integer objects using ==, e.g. Integer a = new Integer(100); Integer b = new Integer(100); System.out.println(a == b);?
o: false, because == compares object references, not values, for these Integer objects
quiz.e: Since a and b are separate Integer objects (not the same reference), == returns false even though their wrapped values are equal; .equals() should be used instead.

quiz.q: What does the .equals() method do differently from == when comparing two ArrayList<String> objects with the same elements in the same order?
o: Nothing different; they behave the same
== checks if they are the same object in memory; .equals() checks whether their contents (elements, order) are equal
equals() is not defined for ArrayList
quiz.e: ArrayList overrides equals() to perform an element-by-element content comparison, whereas == only checks whether both variables reference the identical list object.

quiz.q: What is printed by the following code that builds a list of names and then clears it? ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<String>(); list.add("Al"); list.add("Bo"); list.clear(); System.out.println(list.size());
quiz.e: The clear() method removes all elements from the list, so size() returns 0 afterward.

quiz.q: When a method has a parameter ArrayList<Integer> list and modifies it by calling list.add(5), what happens to the original list passed by the caller?
o: Nothing; it's unaffected since Java is pass by value
The original list is also modified, since the reference passed points to the same object
quiz.e: Because the reference (not a copy of the object) is passed, calling mutating methods like add() on the parameter affects the same object the caller has.

quiz.q: What is the best way to check if an ArrayList<Integer> list is empty before calling list.get(0)?
o: Check if (!list.isEmpty()) or (list.size() > 0) before accessing elements
quiz.e: Checking isEmpty() or size() > 0 before accessing an element avoids an IndexOutOfBoundsException on an empty list.

quiz.q: What is the output of: ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<Integer>(Arrays.asList(3, 1, 4, 1, 5)); Collections.sort(list); System.out.println(list);
quiz.e: Collections.sort() sorts the ArrayList in ascending natural order, producing [1, 1, 3, 4, 5].

quiz.q: How does traversing an ArrayList with an index-based for loop differ syntactically from traversing an array?
o: It is identical, using list[i] just like arr[i]
It uses list.get(i) instead of bracket notation, since ArrayList doesn't overload the [] operator
ArrayLists cannot be traversed with a for loop
quiz.e: ArrayList does not support array bracket syntax; elements must be accessed with the get(i) method inside an index-based loop.

quiz.q: Which scenario is a strong reason to prefer ArrayList over a plain array?
o: You know the exact fixed size in advance and need maximum performance
The number of elements will change frequently during the program's execution (adding/removing)
You are storing primitive types only
quiz.e: ArrayList's dynamic resizing and built-in add/remove methods make it well-suited for situations where the collection size changes over time.

quiz.q: What is the value returned by list.indexOf("x") if "x" is not found in an ArrayList<String>?
quiz.e: indexOf() returns -1 as a sentinel value when the specified element is not present in the list.

quiz.q: What is the result of calling list.add(0, "first") on ArrayList<String> list = ["a", "b"]?
quiz.e: add(index, element) inserts the new element at the specified index, shifting existing elements to the right, resulting in ["first", "a", "b"].

quiz.q: What is the output of: ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<Integer>(); list.add(5); list.add(10); list.add(15); int total = 0; for (int x : list) { total += x; } System.out.println(total);
quiz.e: Summing all elements of the list (5+10+15) gives 30.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of using generics, such as ArrayList<String>, over a raw ArrayList without a type parameter?
o: Generics provide compile-time type checking, preventing accidental insertion of the wrong type and avoiding manual casting when retrieving elements
Generics remove the need for the add method
quiz.e: Specifying a type parameter lets the compiler catch type errors early and removes the need to cast objects retrieved from the list.

quiz.q: What is the output of: ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<String>(); list.add("x"); list.add("y"); list.add("z"); System.out.println(list.get(list.size()-1));
quiz.e: list.size()-1 is the index of the last element, which is "z".

quiz.q: Which is true about passing an ArrayList to a method versus passing an int to a method?
o: The ArrayList reference is copied, but it points to the same underlying object, so mutations are visible to the caller; the int is copied by value and changes inside the method don't affect the caller's variable
Neither can be passed to methods
int is passed by reference in Java
quiz.e: Java is pass-by-value for everything, but for reference types like ArrayList, the value passed is the reference itself, so both caller and method see the same object; primitives like int are copied as independent values.

quiz.q: How do you correctly declare a 2D array of ints with 3 rows and 4 columns?
quiz.e: A 2D array uses double brackets in both the type and the 'new' expression: int[][] arr = new int[3][4];

quiz.q: In a 2D array grid, how do you access the element in row 2, column 3?
quiz.e: 2D array access uses the format array[row][column], so row 2, column 3 is grid[2][3].

quiz.q: What does grid.length return for a 2D array declared as int[][] grid = new int[5][3];?
quiz.e: For a 2D array, .length on the outer array gives the number of rows (the first dimension).

quiz.q: What does grid[0].length return for int[][] grid = new int[5][3];?
o: 3, the number of columns in row 0
quiz.e: grid[0] is itself an array representing the first row, and its .length gives the number of columns in that row, which is 3.

quiz.q: Which nested loop structure correctly visits every element of a 2D array int[][] grid with R rows and C columns?
o: for (int i = 0; i < R; i++) for (int j = 0; j < C; j++) grid[i][j]...
for (int i = 0; i < C; i++) for (int j = 0; j < R; j++) grid[i][j]...
for (int i = 0; i < R; i++) grid[i]...
quiz.e: The outer loop iterates over rows (0 to R-1) and the inner loop iterates over columns (0 to C-1), accessing grid[i][j] correctly.

quiz.q: What is inheritance in object-oriented programming?
o: A mechanism where one class (subclass) acquires fields and methods from another class (superclass)
A way to declare multiple constructors
quiz.e: Inheritance allows a subclass to reuse and extend the fields and methods defined in a superclass, establishing an 'is-a' relationship.

quiz.q: Which keyword is used to indicate that a class inherits from another class in Java?
quiz.e: The 'extends' keyword is used when declaring a class to indicate it is a subclass of another class.

quiz.q: Given: public class Animal { ... } public class Dog extends Animal { ... } what is Dog considered relative to Animal?
o: Dog is the superclass of Animal
Dog is a subclass of Animal, inheriting its members
Animal is a subclass of Dog
quiz.e: Because Dog extends Animal, Dog is the subclass and Animal is the superclass, meaning Dog inherits Animal's non-private members.

quiz.q: What does calling super() as the first line of a subclass constructor do?
o: Invokes the superclass's constructor to initialize inherited fields before the subclass's own initialization runs
quiz.e: super() explicitly invokes the superclass's constructor, ensuring the inherited part of the object is properly initialized first.

quiz.q: What is polymorphism in the context of inheritance, as demonstrated by 'Animal a = new Dog();'?
o: A syntax error, since Dog and Animal are different types
A reference of the supertype can refer to an object of a subtype, allowing overridden methods to run based on the object's actual (dynamic) type
Casting always required for this to work
This only compiles if Dog has no methods
quiz.e: Polymorphism allows a superclass reference to point to a subclass object, and calling an overridden method uses the actual runtime type's version (dynamic method binding).

quiz.q: If Dog overrides Animal's makeSound() method, what happens when you call a.makeSound() where Animal a = new Dog();?
o: Animal's version always runs, since a is declared as Animal
Dog's overridden version runs, because Java uses the object's actual runtime type to decide which method to call
quiz.e: Java uses dynamic (runtime) method dispatch for overridden instance methods, so the actual object's class (Dog) determines which version executes, regardless of the reference's declared type.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the 'protected' access modifier?
o: Only accessible within the exact same class
Accessible within the same class, subclasses, and the same package
quiz.e: 'protected' members are accessible within the declaring class, its subclasses (even in other packages), and other classes in the same package.

quiz.q: What must be true for a subclass method to properly override a superclass method?
o: It must have a different name
It must have the same name, same parameter list, and a compatible return type as the superclass method
It must have a different return type
quiz.e: A valid override requires an identical method signature (name and parameters) to the superclass version, with a covariant or identical return type.

quiz.q: What is the output of: 2D array int[][] grid = {{1,2},{3,4},{5,6}}; System.out.println(grid[2][1]);
quiz.e: grid[2] is the row {5,6}, and grid[2][1] accesses the second element of that row, which is 6.

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly sums all elements of a 2D int array using nested loops?
o: int sum=0; for(int i=0;i<grid.length;i++) for(int j=0;j<grid[i].length;j++) sum+=grid[i][j];
quiz.e: Correctly summing a 2D array requires a nested loop: the outer loop over rows and the inner loop over each row's columns, adding grid[i][j] each time.

quiz.q: What does it mean if a subclass 'is-a' type of its superclass, e.g. a Dog is-a Animal?
o: Dog and Animal share no relationship
Every Dog object can also be treated as an Animal object due to inheritance, satisfying the substitution principle
Animal objects can be treated as Dog objects
This is only true for interfaces
quiz.e: The is-a relationship means a subclass object can be used anywhere its superclass type is expected, since it inherits and extends that type's capabilities.

quiz.q: If a subclass wants to call an overridden method's original superclass version, what syntax is used?
quiz.e: The 'super' keyword lets a subclass explicitly call the superclass's version of a method it has overridden.

quiz.q: What happens if a class extends another class but does not override any of its methods?
o: The subclass simply inherits and uses the superclass's implementations as-is
quiz.e: Without any overrides, calling an inherited method on the subclass object simply runs the superclass's original implementation.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following jagged array access? int[][] jagged = {{1}, {2,3}, {4,5,6}}; System.out.println(jagged[2].length);
quiz.e: In a jagged array, each row can have a different length; row index 2 is {4,5,6}, which has length 3.

quiz.q: Which best describes a jagged 2D array in Java?
o: A 2D array where every row must have the same number of columns
A 2D array where different rows can have different numbers of columns
An array that cannot be used with loops
quiz.e: Unlike a strictly rectangular 2D array, a jagged array allows each row (sub-array) to have its own independent length.

quiz.q: Given a superclass Shape with method double getArea() and subclass Circle overriding getArea(), what does the following print? Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(2) }; System.out.println(shapes[0].getArea());
o: It calls Shape's version of getArea()
It calls Circle's overridden version of getArea(), due to dynamic dispatch
quiz.e: Even though the array is typed as Shape[], each element's actual runtime type (Circle) determines which overridden method executes.

quiz.q: Which access modifier allows a superclass field to be directly accessed by a subclass but not by unrelated classes outside the package?
quiz.e: 'protected' grants access to subclasses (even in different packages) and same-package classes, while blocking unrelated outside classes.

quiz.q: What is the effect of declaring a superclass method as 'private'?
o: It can be overridden normally by subclasses
It cannot be inherited or overridden by subclasses at all, since subclasses can't even see it
It becomes accessible to all classes
quiz.e: Private members are not inherited in the usual sense—subclasses cannot see or override them because they are not visible outside the declaring class.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int[][] grid = new int[3][3]; for (int i=0;i<3;i++) for (int j=0;j<3;j++) grid[i][j] = i + j; System.out.println(grid[2][1]);
quiz.e: grid[2][1] is set to i+j where i=2 and j=1, giving 2+1=3.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship established using 'implements' with an interface, compared to 'extends' with a class?
o: They are functionally identical in every way
'implements' is used for a class to fulfill an interface's contract (method signatures), while 'extends' establishes a class inheritance hierarchy
'extends' cannot be used with abstract classes
quiz.e: 'implements' connects a class to an interface it must fully define the methods for, whereas 'extends' creates a superclass-subclass inheritance relationship.

quiz.q: What is the output of using the .equals() method versus overriding toString() when printing a subclass object that inherits Object's default equals but overrides toString?
o: Both use the inherited default automatically
println uses the overridden toString() for the object's text representation, while equals() (not overridden) still compares object references
quiz.e: Overriding only toString() customizes what gets printed, while equals() retains the inherited (default) reference-comparison behavior unless it's separately overridden.

quiz.q: When traversing a rectangular 2D array to print it row by row, what is a correct approach?
o: for (int i=0;i<grid.length;i++){ for(int j=0;j<grid[i].length;j++) System.out.print(grid[i][j]+" "); System.out.println(); }
quiz.e: Printing a 2D array row by row requires nested loops: an outer loop for rows and an inner loop to print each column value, with a newline after each row.

quiz.q: What does calling a constructor of a subclass automatically do regarding the superclass?
o: Nothing related to the superclass happens
It implicitly or explicitly invokes a superclass constructor (via super() or an automatic default call) before running its own body
quiz.e: Every subclass constructor's first action (implicit or explicit) is to invoke a superclass constructor, ensuring inherited fields are properly initialized.

quiz.q: Which best explains why overriding requires the exact same parameter list as the superclass method, while overloading requires a different one?
o: Overriding is about the compiler picking a version at compile time; overloading is dynamic
Overriding replaces the inherited behavior for the same method signature so it's substitutable at runtime; overloading defines distinct methods differentiated by their parameters
Only overloading exists in Java, not overriding
quiz.e: Overriding must exactly match the signature so calls resolve polymorphically to the subclass version at runtime, while overloading depends on distinct parameter lists resolved at compile time.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following code accessing a partially filled 2D array (jagged) row lengths? int[][] a = {{1,2,3},{4},{5,6}}; int total=0; for(int[] row: a) total += row.length; System.out.println(total);
quiz.e: The row lengths are 3, 1, and 2, which sum to 6.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int[][] a = new int[2][2]; a[0][0]=1; a[0][1]=2; a[1][0]=3; a[1][1]=4; int sum=0; for(int[] row: a) for(int val: row) sum+=val; System.out.println(sum);
quiz.e: Summing all four elements 1+2+3+4 gives 10.

quiz.q: Why is dynamic method binding (also called dynamic dispatch) important for polymorphism to work correctly?
o: It ensures the compiler always picks the superclass method
It ensures that at runtime, the actual object's class determines which overridden method executes, not the reference's declared type
It only matters for static methods
quiz.e: Dynamic dispatch is what allows a superclass-typed reference to correctly invoke a subclass's overridden method based on the object's real, runtime type.

quiz.q: What is the output of: class A { public String toString(){return "A";} } class B extends A { public String toString(){return "B";} } A obj = new B(); System.out.println(obj);
quiz.e: Since obj actually refers to a B object, and toString() is overridden, dynamic dispatch calls B's version, printing "B".

quiz.q: What is the output of the following, iterating a rectangular 2D array by columns rather than rows? int[][] grid = {{1,2},{3,4}}; for (int j=0;j<2;j++){ for(int i=0;i<2;i++){ System.out.print(grid[i][j]); } }
quiz.e: Fixing j=0 first and varying i prints grid[0][0]=1, grid[1][0]=3, then for j=1 prints grid[0][1]=2, grid[1][1]=4, giving "1324".

quiz.q: What must a subclass constructor do if its superclass has no no-argument constructor (only a constructor requiring parameters)?
o: It must explicitly call super(args) with matching arguments as its first statement, since Java cannot supply a default no-arg call
It must override the superclass constructor
quiz.e: If the superclass has no no-argument constructor, the subclass must explicitly invoke an existing superclass constructor via super(args) matching one of its signatures.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int[][] grid = {{1,2,3},{4,5,6}}; System.out.println(grid.length + "," + grid[0].length);
quiz.e: grid.length is the number of rows (2), and grid[0].length is the number of columns in row 0 (3), giving "2,3".

quiz.q: Which of the following is true when a subclass method has the same name as a superclass method but a different parameter list?
o: This is overloading, not overriding, since the parameter lists differ
This is only legal for static methods
quiz.e: Because overriding requires an identical parameter list, a differing parameter list makes this a new overloaded method rather than an override.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int[][] a = {{1,2},{3,4}}; int[][] b = a; b[0][0] = 99; System.out.println(a[0][0]);
quiz.e: Since 2D arrays are reference types, b = a makes b alias the same array as a, so modifying b[0][0] also changes what a sees, printing 99.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes an abstract class in relation to inheritance?
o: A class that cannot be extended by any subclass
A class that cannot be instantiated directly and may contain abstract methods that subclasses must implement
A class with only static methods
A class that must implement every method with a body
quiz.e: An abstract class serves as a partial blueprint: it cannot be instantiated on its own, and it may declare abstract methods that concrete subclasses are required to override.

quiz.q: What is the output of: int[][] grid = new int[2][3]; System.out.println(grid[1][2]);
quiz.e: Numeric 2D array elements default to 0, so an unassigned int element like grid[1][2] is 0.

quiz.q: What is a base case in a recursive method?
o: The case that causes infinite recursion
A condition that stops the recursive calls and returns a result directly, without further recursion
quiz.e: The base case is the simplest scenario in a recursive method that can be answered directly, halting further recursive calls and preventing infinite recursion.

quiz.q: What is the most likely result of a recursive method that has no base case, or whose base case is never reached?
o: It eventually causes a StackOverflowError due to infinite recursive calls
quiz.e: Without a base case that is eventually reached, recursive calls continue indefinitely, exhausting the call stack and causing a StackOverflowError.

quiz.q: Consider: public static int factorial(int n) { if (n == 0) return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1); } What is factorial(4)?
quiz.e: factorial(4) = 4 * factorial(3) = 4 * 3 * factorial(2) = ... = 4*3*2*1*1 = 24.

quiz.q: In the recursive factorial method, what is the base case?
quiz.e: The base case 'if (n == 0) return 1;' provides a direct answer without further recursive calls, stopping the recursion.

quiz.q: What does the recursive case of a recursive method typically do?
o: Breaks the problem into a smaller version of itself and calls the method again on that smaller version
quiz.e: The recursive case reduces the problem to a smaller subproblem and calls the method recursively on that smaller input, progressing toward the base case.

quiz.q: Consider: public static int sum(int n) { if (n <= 0) return 0; return n + sum(n - 1); } What is sum(3)?
What data structure implicitly tracks recursive calls waiting to complete, storing each call's local variables and return address?
quiz.e: Each recursive call is pushed onto the call stack, which stores that call's state until it returns, at which point it's popped off.

quiz.q: What is the output of the following recursive method call? public static void printDown(int n) { if (n <= 0) return; System.out.print(n + " "); printDown(n - 1); } printDown(3);
quiz.e: The method prints n before recursing on n-1, so it prints 3, then 2, then 1, before hitting the base case at n=0.

quiz.q: What is the output of: public static void printUp(int n) { if (n <= 0) return; printUp(n - 1); System.out.print(n + " "); } printUp(3);
quiz.e: Since the recursive call happens before the print statement, the deepest calls print first, unwinding to print 1, then 2, then 3.

quiz.q: What is recursive Fibonacci: public static int fib(int n) { if (n <= 1) return n; return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2); } What is fib(5)?
quiz.e: fib(5) = fib(4) + fib(3) = ... following the sequence 0,1,1,2,3,5, fib(5) equals 5.

quiz.q: What is a key inefficiency of the naive recursive Fibonacci implementation for larger n?
o: It recomputes the same subproblems repeatedly, leading to exponential time complexity
It only works for even n
quiz.e: Without memoization, the naive recursive approach recalculates identical fib(k) values many times, resulting in exponential O(2^n) time complexity.

quiz.q: How can recursion be used to implement binary search on a sorted array?
o: It's impossible; binary search must be iterative
The method calls itself on either the left or right half of the array (a smaller subarray) based on comparing the target to the middle element, until the base case (found or empty range) is reached
quiz.e: A recursive binary search reduces the search range by half each call, recursing into the appropriate half until the target is found or the range becomes empty (base case).

quiz.q: What is the relationship between recursion and iteration (loops)?
o: They can never solve the same problems
Many problems solvable by loops can also be solved recursively, and vice versa, though one approach may be more natural or efficient for a given problem
Recursion is always faster than loops
quiz.e: Recursion and iteration are both mechanisms for repetition, and many problems can be expressed with either approach, though efficiency and clarity may differ.

quiz.q: What is the base case for a recursive method that reverses a String, such as public static String reverse(String s) { if (s.length() <= 1) return s; return reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0); }?
o: s.length() <= 1, returning s directly since a string of length 0 or 1 is already its own reverse
quiz.e: A string of length 0 or 1 reversed is itself, so this condition directly returns the answer without further recursive calls.

quiz.q: What does the recursive method call reverse("cat") ultimately build, step by step, using reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0)?
quiz.e: Recursively peeling off the first character and appending it at the end reverses the string: reverse("cat") builds "tac".

quiz.q: What is meant by an algorithm's 'divide and conquer' strategy, often implemented recursively?
o: Solving a problem entirely with one large computation
Breaking a problem into smaller subproblems, solving each recursively, and combining their results
quiz.e: Divide and conquer algorithms (like merge sort or recursive binary search) split a problem into smaller pieces, solve them (often recursively), and merge the results.

quiz.q: In merge sort, what is the base case for the recursive sorting of a sub-array?
o: A sub-array of length 0 or 1, which is already trivially sorted
The sub-array must be sorted manually first
quiz.e: A sub-array with 0 or 1 elements is inherently already sorted, so merge sort's recursion stops there and begins merging results back together.

quiz.q: What two main steps does merge sort perform after dividing an array into two halves recursively?
o: Sort each half and merge the two sorted halves into one sorted array
quiz.e: After recursively sorting each half, merge sort combines (merges) the two sorted halves into a single sorted array by comparing elements in order.

quiz.q: What is the overall time complexity of merge sort?
quiz.e: Merge sort divides the array in half at each level (log n levels) and does O(n) work merging at each level, giving O(n log n) overall.

quiz.q: How does merge sort's time complexity compare to selection sort's or bubble sort's O(n^2) for large arrays?
o: Merge sort is generally more efficient for large n, since n log n grows slower than n^2
quiz.e: Because n log n grows much more slowly than n^2 as n increases, merge sort scales better and is generally faster than selection or bubble sort for large inputs.

quiz.q: Consider a recursive method to compute the sum of digits of a positive integer: public static int digitSum(int n) { if (n < 10) return n; return n % 10 + digitSum(n / 10); } What is digitSum(123)?
quiz.e: digitSum(123) = 3 + digitSum(12) = 3 + (2 + digitSum(1)) = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

quiz.q: What must be true about each recursive call's argument relative to the base case for the recursion to eventually terminate?
o: The argument can be anything, including unchanged values
The argument must progress (get closer) toward the base case with each successive call
Recursion always terminates regardless of the argument
quiz.e: For recursion to terminate correctly, each call must move the input closer to a base case (e.g., decreasing n, or shrinking an array), otherwise infinite recursion results.

quiz.q: What is the output of: public static int mystery(int n) { if (n == 1) return 1; if (n % 2 == 0) return mystery(n / 2); else return mystery(3 * n + 1); } (conceptually, what recursive process does this resemble?)
o: The Collatz conjecture sequence, repeatedly halving even numbers or applying 3n+1 to odd numbers until reaching 1
quiz.e: This recursive pattern—halving even numbers or computing 3n+1 for odd numbers until reaching 1—is the classic Collatz conjecture sequence.

quiz.q: Why is it generally considered good practice to check the base case before making the recursive call in a recursive method?
o: It's not important where the base case check is placed
Checking it first ensures the method returns immediately for the simplest cases, preventing unnecessary or infinite recursive calls
It makes the method run in a loop instead
It only matters for void methods
quiz.e: Placing the base case check first avoids making the recursive call when it's unnecessary, correctly stopping the recursion right when the terminal condition is met.

quiz.q: What is the value of the recursive call fib(3) using fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2), fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1?
Which of the following problems is naturally well-suited to a recursive solution because of its self-similar substructure?
o: Computing the nth Fibonacci number, since fib(n) is defined in terms of fib(n-1) and fib(n-2)
Reading a single integer from input
quiz.e: Fibonacci numbers are naturally defined recursively (fib(n) depends on the two prior Fibonacci numbers), making a recursive solution a direct match to the problem's structure.

quiz.q: What is the correct recursive method to compute the length of a String s without using .length()? public static int myLength(String s) { if (s.equals("")) return ___; return 1 + myLength(s.substring(1)); }
quiz.e: An empty string has length 0, which is the correct base case value to return directly.

quiz.q: What does the expression 'binary search reduces the problem size by half with each recursive call' imply about its recursion depth for an array of size n?
o: The recursion depth is approximately log2(n)
quiz.e: Since each call halves the remaining search space, the maximum number of recursive calls before reaching a base case is about log2(n).

quiz.q: What is the output of: public static int power(int base, int exp) { if (exp == 0) return 1; return base * power(base, exp - 1); } power(2, 4)?
In the recursive power method above, what is the base case and why is it necessary?
o: exp == 0, returning 1, since any base raised to the 0th power is 1, and this stops further recursive multiplication
There is no base case needed
quiz.e: The base case exp == 0 (returning 1, matching the mathematical fact that x^0 = 1) is required to terminate the recursive calls that otherwise keep decrementing exp.

quiz.q: Which of these best describes recursive backtracking, such as used to explore all subsets or permutations?
o: A method that explores possible choices recursively, undoing (backtracking) a choice if it doesn't lead to a solution, to try another
A single loop that never checks conditions
A method with no base case
quiz.e: Backtracking recursively tries a choice, recurses further, and if that path fails or after exploring it, undoes the choice and tries alternative options.

quiz.q: What is a potential downside of using recursion instead of iteration for simple repetitive tasks?
o: Recursion is always illegal in Java
Recursion can use more memory (call stack space) and may be less efficient due to function call overhead, compared to a straightforward loop
quiz.e: Each recursive call adds a frame to the call stack, consuming memory and incurring function-call overhead, which can make recursion less efficient than an equivalent loop for simple tasks.

quiz.q: Consider a recursive method to check if an array is sorted: public static boolean isSorted(int[] arr, int index) { if (index >= arr.length - 1) return true; if (arr[index] > arr[index+1]) return false; return isSorted(arr, index + 1); } What does the base case index >= arr.length - 1 represent?
o: Reaching the last element (or beyond), meaning there are no more adjacent pairs left to compare, so the array is considered sorted
quiz.e: Once index reaches or passes the second-to-last position, there are no more adjacent pairs to check, so if no violation has been found, the array must be sorted.

quiz.q: What is the output of: public static int gcd(int a, int b) { if (b == 0) return a; return gcd(b, a % b); } gcd(48, 18)?
quiz.e: Using the Euclidean algorithm: gcd(48,18)=gcd(18,12)=gcd(12,6)=gcd(6,0)=6.

quiz.q: What principle underlies the correctness of well-designed recursive methods, often proven using induction?
o: If the base case is correct and each recursive case correctly reduces to a valid smaller instance whose correctness is assumed, then the whole method is correct for all valid inputs
Recursion is always correct by definition
Recursive methods cannot be proven correct
Only iterative methods can be verified
quiz.e: Similar to mathematical induction, verifying a recursive method involves confirming the base case is correct and that each recursive step correctly builds on the assumption that smaller subproblems are already solved correctly.

quiz.q: What is the output of: public static int sumArray(int[] arr, int index) { if (index == arr.length) return 0; return arr[index] + sumArray(arr, index + 1); } sumArray(new int[]{1,2,3,4}, 0)?
quiz.e: The recursive calls add each element from index 0 to 3, summing 1+2+3+4=10, with the base case returning 0 once index reaches the array's length.

quiz.q: What is the output of: public static int countDown(int n) { if (n <= 0) { System.out.println("Liftoff!"); return 0; } System.out.println(n); return countDown(n - 1); } countDown(2); (what is printed, in order)?
quiz.e: The method prints n (2) before recursing, then prints 1, and finally reaches the base case which prints "Liftoff!", in that order.

quiz.q: Which statement best distinguishes 'recursive case' from 'base case' in a recursive method's design?
o: The base case makes the recursive call; the recursive case terminates it
The base case directly handles the simplest input(s) without further recursion; the recursive case reduces the problem and calls the method again
Only the base case is required; the recursive case is optional
quiz.e: A correctly designed recursive method needs a base case for direct termination and a recursive case that shrinks the problem toward that base case.

quiz.q: What would likely happen if the recursive case in a Fibonacci method called fib(n-1) and fib(n+1) instead of fib(n-1) and fib(n-2)?
o: It would likely never reach the base case in the fib(n+1) branch, causing infinite recursion and a StackOverflowError
It would only affect even n
quiz.e: Calling fib(n+1) moves away from the base case rather than toward it, so that branch of recursion would never terminate, leading to a stack overflow.

quiz.q: In a recursive binary search, what does the base case return when the target is not found (i.e., low > high)?
o: A signal value such as -1 indicating the target was not found
The first index of the array
quiz.e: When the search bounds cross (low exceeds high), there's nothing left to search, so the base case returns a sentinel like -1 to indicate the target isn't present.

A way of describing an algorithm's worst-case growth rate as input size increases, e.g. O(n), O(log n), O(n^2).
